title: Ravens Least Experienced Corner Could Be Most Vital Sunday vs Browns. Here's Why
full_text:
If the Ravens were facing Zay Flowers in some parallel universe, and he was lining up in the slot, which of Baltimore’s defensive backs do you think would draw the coverage responsibility?
Who would share enough commonality in terms of build and twitch and leverage to be able to hang with a jitterbug like that, or attempt try to hang with a jitterbug like that, where he has a two-way go and the entire middle of the field to work? Most likely, that would be rookie nickel corner Chandler Rivers. And while Cleveland’s rookie wideout KC Concepcion is not at the level of Flowers, Browns head coach Todd Monken, former Ravens offensive coordinator , is using him inn] a very similar way and Cleveland’s diverse passing attack is stacked in ways that present Baltimore’s sagging secondary potentially serious problems.
Monken will come at Baltimore with vigor – the Ravens are bracing for as much – and they will be throwing the ball quite a bit and there will likely be multiple match-ups that decide this game on this side of the ball. But it stands to reason that Rivers, a fifth-round pick, and Concepcion, who was selected 24th overall, will see quite a bit of one another and while Rivers has done some very nice things as a rookie and has great instincts reading screens and wrapping up when the play is in front of, like the rest of this allegedly-elite secondary, he has been picked up in coverage in recent weeks and it’s a major issue for this team across the board .
The Ravens tackling in the secondary has suffered and the Browns defense is heavily reliant on yards after the catch (8th in the NFL in YAC/reception) and Concepcion is someone with the athletic skillset to burn you just that way.
“You have to take great angles,” Ravens coach Jesse Minter said of the challenge. “You have to be super detailed when you're tackling these guys in the open field — attacking the right hip with the right leverage, knowing where your help is.
“You're never out there by yourself, and so it's knowing, if he does cut back or you miss it, where's your help, and where are those things at? It's a detail game in open-field tackling. They do a great job with the ball after the catch … Good group of skill players that can make plays, and a challenge we're excited about."
The Ravens corners have been bad in coverage against mostly marginal quarterbacks to this point, as we have been documenting. Ravens corners and free safeties in coverage:
Opposing QBs: 70/100 (70%), 836 yards (11.9/comp), 5 TDs – 0 INTs, 111.9 rating
13 passes 20+, 41 1st downs, 3 DPI, 4 pass breakups
Yeah, that sucks. But it gets even worse when you drill down on what happens in coverage on targets who come from the slot:
Opposing QBs : 37/50 (74%, 24th in NFL), 9.1 yds/att (23rd), 3 TD – 0 INT, 121.8 rating (25th).
Concepcion is in the slot on 60% of his snaps, far and away most on the Browns.
He does the most damage from the slot. And overall, he sees 20% of the team’s targets, tied with fellow rookie Denzel Boston, with elite move tight Harold Fannin at 18% (running back Quinshon Judkins is next at 14%). The Ravens don’t usually move corners around with someone, but could bring top outside corner Nate Wiggins into the slot for Concepcion. However, that might create bigger problems on the outside, and Minter has been very reticent to use veteran Chidobe Awuzie out there and probably for good reason.
“We don’t necessarily have to travel to people,” defensive coordinator Anthony Weaver noted on Thursday in discussing this difficult match-up for his secondary.
Rivers is playing quite a bit, he is a quintessential slot guy, and in the last three weeks he’s allowed nine catches on 11 targets for 120 yards and touchdown. Gulp.
The Ravens also have struggled to defend No. 1 wide receivers all season and when they did face one team that had two real wideouts who could win – Dallas – both got off on this defense. The return of top pass rusher Trey Hendrickson from a finger injury should add juice to the pass rush, but the Ravens are going to keep hearing questions about receivers getting over on them until they do something about it.
“We’ve had our good days and our bad days,” Weaver suggested, which is whimsical and all but not quite true. And Monken is uniquely qualified to spot their underbelly and knows most of these players quite well and we suspect Rivers will be in his sights.
Since Week 2, here is what quality receivers have done to this defense:
Drake London (ATL): 7/11, 118 yards, 7 1st D
Carnell Tate (TEN) : 9/12, 145 yds, 6 1st D
CeeDee Lamb (DAL): 7/8, 112 yds 5 1st D
George Pickens (DAL): 7/11, 82 yds, 4 1st D
Chris Olave (NO): 8/10, 86 yds, TD, 6 1st D
The Browns are very aware. Monken knows .
“They have some guys that can stretch the field and do some things in short areas,” corner Marlon Humphrey said of the Browns. “They have a lot of talent over there, and it will be all -hands-on-deck to try to kind of contain the offense."

title: Report Card For Ravens Rookie Play Caller After 5 Games: Straight A's?
full_text:
The greatest unknown for the 2027 Baltimore Ravens – a team that was changing its identity in a major way for the first time in nearly 20 years with John Harbaigh gone as coach -was on the offensive side of the ball.
The greatest risks with this team, in terms of roster and coaching, came on offense, with first-time play caller Declan Doyle, basically the same age as quarterback Lamar Jackson , taking the reigns for the first time, implementing an offense that did not previously exist and doing it with some very significant questions about the interior of the offensive line. The degree of difficulty for Doyle was already significant – would anyone besides Zay Flowers make plays downfield?  – and it ramped up further with that offensive line repeatedly collapsing and Baltimore entering Week 6 looking at perhaps it’s sixth different combination of starting linemen.
Oh, and the defense that was supposed to carry the team early has been mostly meh, and it’s already blown two 11-point leads that Doyle’s unit built, and a secondary loaded with top draft picks and huge contracts has been largely suspect in coverage so far . Special teams blunders also had plenty to do with the team’s lone loss (4-1), and Doyle has had to operate without Flowers for large chunks of games or one game entirely, and his alleged move tight end (Mark Andrews on a silly contract extension) can’t actually move much and his left tackle missed time and Lamar Jackson didn’t play last week and hasn’t practiced fully in quite some time.
“There’s challenges every week, whether it’s at quarterback or different wideouts, or different tight ends as you lose guys throughout the year,” Doyle said Thursday before practice. “I’ve said it to the group, ‘It’s all about fixing this week’s problems.'”
And Doyle has navigated it all overwhelmingly with tremendous Aplomb. No, that’s not a typo (though heaven knows I make my share) – that “A” is capitalized for a reason. I’m tempted to go with an A+ here, honestly, but it’s still a little early for that. It’s been a pretty Amazing start, and here’s some of what stood out in him earning that grade:
So some fears were confirmed – at least so far – about Andrews being cooked and the lack of a go-to pass catcher for chunk yards besides Flowers. But man, if he’s going to be a one-man army, let him do it in truly historic fashion where he is showing up in the endzone and in the redzone like never before. And cashing in. His five redzone targets are already half of last season’s total and he’s on pace to shatter his career high of 13 (remember he’s only run 91 routes all season due to injury).
Doyle has already used flowers three times as much in the backfield as he was deployed there ALL OF LAST SEASON, and made sage adjustments to the perimeter run game when in IOL cratered. He ramped Flowers slot usage from 38% in his first three years to 52% this season and he’s been close to unstoppable with a two-way go there.
Flowers has produced like a top five receiver and given that Rashod Bateman remains mostly a decoy and Devontez Walker is super fringy and rookie start Ja’Kobi Lane has played one half of football all season due to injury and Andrews and Bateman lead this team in route runs by a mile with little to show for it because of the injuries, they’ve needed that sort of ascent from an already very good football player.
For all the explosion in this attack and with Doyle rightfully backing up Flowers and Jackson calling him a “genius” this summer, by and large, managing games and managing the clock and playing complimentary football with a struggling defense matters greatly. And it can be very hard for some young coordinators to live with “three-yards-and-a-cloud of dust” when dictated by margin, down, distance, game flow, time remaining.
The personnel problems have put Doyle in situations where repeatedly the KISS method – not pyro makeup; just Keep It Simple Stupid – is what was required and he's leaned into that and accepted the ugliness in the stats that come with it. The fact that Derrick Henry has run more times through five games than any 32-year-old running back since the 1970 merger speaks to that (and that despite Henry sporting a league-average 4.2 yards/carry and not the 5.5/carry from his first two years here).
He’s understood by and large the significant limitations of this offensive line at times and tried to help them out. Recently losing “Joker” blocking tight end Durham Smythe was another hue blow and Doyle had some interesting workarounds in the game plan in Sunday’s comeback win at Atlanta. He also brought along back-up Snoop Huntley in a smart, old-school manner in that game and didn’t have him attacking the middle of the field until the final two-minute drill, and he’s woven Henry more into the screen game than before to help combat pass-protection issues and a bogged-down run game at times.
“I think he is the most brilliant offensive mind in football right now,“ right tackle Roger Rosengarten said. “I think he's done a great job with weaving in those play calls when the right time is called. I think anytime you call a screen, it's about time and operation with those sorts of things. Dec is one-of-one at calling them and making sure they're called at the right times.”
Doyle isn’t repeating the same mistakes over and over. That hasn’t always been the case around here.
When it becomes clear that trying to run between the tackles isn’t going great, he adjusts. When he takes the ball out of Henry’s hands and Lamar’s hands in critical third downs of what became a loss against the Saints, and his offensive line gets further compromised by injury, he leans into old-school stuff on the ground. He has to get major credit – along with the entire staff and especially OL coach Dwayne Ledford – for getting rookie guard Vega Ioane to perform so admirably thrust into center with difficult defensive assignments.
He’s using more pre-snap motion and cadence than ever before, he installed the under-center offense we knew was coming and, yes, there have been too many penalties in part because of some of that, but this offense is exceling on early downs despite all those issues and they are finishing drives despite some short-yardage issues.
The Ravens rank fourth in points scored and sixth in total Offensive Expected Points Added and sixth in points/drive and Jackson looks primed for another MVP run. If Doyle keeps this up, the buzz for possible head coaching openings will be very real by Christmas, maybe even Thanksgiving.
We’ll have another progress report by then.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: 4 Reasons The Browns Could Upset The Ravens Sunday
full_text:
The Ravens have a way of coming up small in Cleveland.
Weird things happen. They tend to undermine themselves. And now they have this Todd Monken thing to deal with, as Baltimore’s former offensive coordinator was pushed out as part of John Harbaugh’s staff only to land as the Browns head coach. Cleveland already has one upset divisional win, beating the Steelers on a Thursday night, and they will be focused for this game coming off a letdown at the Jets on Sunday.
This will be Ravens rookie head coach Jesse Minter’s first AFC North game, the Ravens are once against dealing with a cumbersome injury report (19 names listed on Wednesday really is something) and it’s no sure thing that Lamar Jackson starts at quarterback despite how some want to couch it.
Every game the Ravens have played this season has ended up pretty snug by the fourth quarter, even the two in which they opened up an 11-point lead, and there is reason to believe the Browns (3-2) can hang around and put some pressure on the Ravens (4-1). And maybe even pull off the upset.
Here are the primary reasons why:
The Browns have a diverse pass game right now with some guys who can get deep and guys who win with YAC and underneath stuff and a move tight end who creates real problems on third down and in the redzone and the Ravens are having big issues there. They are young and fast, and that will present problems even with a weak QB. The Ravens have mostly faced weak QBs.
Baltimore’s corners and free safeties haven’t really been able to cover anyone this season and Monken will not be afraid to chuck the ball all over the yard. And given Cleveland’s extreme issues running the ball , all the more reason to attack a secondary that has suffered. The film and the data is rough, Minter has been exposed in dime coverage and maybe a ramped up pass rush will be the difference but even suspect NFL QBs are  not afraid to challenge the Ravens corners.
"They are explosive," free safety Malaki Starks said. "I think they do a lot within the offense, and they create explosive plays, so that is definitely something that we want to stay on top of."
Monken knows how to motivate a team and he has these young Browns eating out of his hand right now and he’d love nothing more than the beat the Ravens, who fired him and a front officed that made it pretty clear it believed the last coaching staff was holding back their roster. Oh, and the Ravens skill guys were calling Monken’s replacement, 30-year-old Declan Doyle, a “genius” all summer in what looked like shade at the former guy.
Monken will call this game in a let-it-all-hang-out manner and hold nothing back. Look out for some trick plays, maybe a fake punt. He knows most of this Ravens roster pretty well. How they play and how many of them think. Should be an advantage for him.
"I think their offense will definitely try to come at us, and I think their defense will too," Ravens corner Marlon Humphrey said. "Their defense is always really good, but their offense, with the versatility that [Browns head coach] Todd [Monken] calls games, we will have our hands full."
The Ravens are getting strong play from young guard-turned-center-turned-guard Vega Ioane. Like, astonishingly good stuff under the circumstances. But the GM made a panic move and overpaid for the Eagles center-turned-guard/injury-liability Cam Jurgens and they really want to jam him in the middle of the offensive line Sunday.
Except, well, he still doesn’t really know anyone yet and hasn’t ever practiced with the team and they traded for him while he was still in the concussion protocol (which is why other GMs were telling me Eric DeCosta looks incredibly desperate here ). So, even if Jurgens practices close to full Thursday, that’s the last real work day of the week and everything is so new and different, do they really need to rush this?
And if they do, and if Jurgens isn’t nearly as ready to hold down center as Ioane was, and if a sixth-straight different offensive line combination creates havoc and the interior isn’t connected and the A Gap becomes a problem, against a game Cleveland defense, that’s a great way to blow a game.
"There's kind of some unfamiliarity, and it's kind of hard to get in the groove sometimes," right tackle Roger Rosengarten said of the constantly changing lineups. "But if we're all playing together and are all on the same page, good things will happen."
They call Cleveland the Factory of Sadness and it’s truly remarkable just how little good has come to this franchise since the Browns emerged from relocation to Baltimore as an expansion team. It’s been incredibly bleak and the one-sided nature of this rivalry – the Ravens win two Super Bowls and Cleveland is still waiting for its first – makes it even tougher.
But over the last decade, a lot of weird stuff has happened to the Ravens in Cleveland. Guys getting hurt. Players dropping interceptions in rampant succession. Ugly, upset losses. It tends to be a struggle, and the crowd is always up for these games and throw in the Monken thing and the gutsy the young Browns have displayed and there is reason to believe this could be anything but a blowout.
"I am hoping that trend ends Sunday," Humphrey said, "but it is just a hard place to play. I think, like you said, it has just always been weird ... There have just been all types of things that have happened in Cleveland. I think one year, maybe when I was a rookie, we threw maybe two interceptions on the 5-yard line. Just crazy things happen, but the biggest thing is stay together."
The Browns are 4-4 in their last eight at home against the Ravens. This is the sixth time in the last nine meetings where Baltimore is a favorite of three points or more. The Browns get up for these games and only three of these eight games were decided by more than a touchdown.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: Ravens Continue To Exorcise Demons Of Past Failures With Falcons Win
full_text:
The Baltimore Ravens went in a different direction at head coach after having John Harbaugh at the helm for nearly two decades was that in recent years, in no small part because his teams kept finding ways to lose games.
Whether it was blowing double-digit or fourth-quarter leads, coming out flat in games they were favored to win or not being able to find ways to pull off and close out comebacks, they became more synonymous with choking than being clutch.
Just five games into the Jesse Minter era, as just the fourth head coach in franchise history, the Ravens have already shown that they're not letting the tendencies that led to shortcomings in the past determine future outcomes.
They held onto a double-digit lead against a talented offense on the road in Week 1, orchestrated the fastest game-winning drive in NFL history at seven seconds in Week 3 and ground out a one-score win in Week 4 despite getting shut out and losing their starting quarterback for the entire second half.
This past Sunday, they went on the road to face what had been one of the hottest teams of the previous two weeks, without their highest-paid players on both sides of the ball available, including Lamar Jackson, and still found themselves on the right side of history again.
With their 30-23 comeback victory over the Atlanta Falcons in overtime in Week 5, the Ravens became the first team to win a game down by eight or more points in the final minute in four years, which, according to E SPN's Jamison Hensley per ESPN Research , snapped a 581-game losing streak for teams that found themselves in those situations.
After hauling in the game-winning interception and his first since  Week 17 of the 2024 season, three-time All Pro safety Kyle Hamilton didn't mince words when talking about the significance of this win not only for him being back in his hometown of Atlanta but for the Ravens as a whole team and their revamped culture under Minter.
"That is a game that we have lost many times. Whether it is, some fluky stuff happening or whatever," Hamilton said. "That is just us getting over some sort of hump or dark cloud. I am excited for the future."
Even the Ravens' lone setback of the season thus far, when they lost to the New Oreleans Saints in their Week 2 home opener , in which they opened the fourth quarter with an eight-point lead, only to get outscored 15-0 in the final period, served a purpose in the maturation of this year's team.
"Confidence is gained by going through things and going through things together, and I do not know if we would have the results of the last three weeks if the Saints game did not happen," Minter said. "I think there are always ways you can take losses like that. You can learn from them and really try to improve, get better, look at the things that you did well and build on things. I think we did that after that game."
Despite looking like the more physical and well-prepared team out of the gate, with the offense moving the ball well with backup quarterback Tyler Huntley and the defense forcing three straight three-and-outs, the Ravens' win in Atlanta was anything but a cakewalk. They had to overcome adversity in the form of bad drops, a fumble recovery returned for a touchdown against them and the Falcons getting hot on third-and-long, starting in the second quarter.
Even when at full strength with their two-time league MVP healthy and under center, the Ravens found ways to lose the type of games rather than find a way to come out on top. The fact they're finding ways to finish late in games with quick or time-consuming drives, coupled with a few key stops on defense, is evidence that these aren't the same old Ravens whose downfall felt inevitable at times because they hadn't consistently shown an ability to be at their best when their best is required.
"[With] this particular team, to be able to do that, I think is definitely a major benefit to the psyche, the confidence and the belief that we can win games like that in the fourth quarter," Minter said.
After avoiding some close calls with prominent players during training camp and preseason, the Ravens were hit extremely hard with the injury bug over the first month of the season. They had standout rookie wide receiver Ja'Kobi Lane suffer a fractured wrist that required surgery in the season opener, lost their top two centers in the same game in Week 3 and had prized free agent addition, four-time Pro Bowl edge rusher Trey Hendrickson, suffer a finger injury that caused him to miss the last two games while recovering from a minor procedure.
While their initial injury report on Wednesday looked a mile long with nearly two dozen names, the fact that it featured several key players with encouraging status designations is a sign good news on the horizon.
Wednesday's Injury Report pic.twitter.com/OnTJmaKHOD
Although Jackson missed his fourth straight practice with the ankle sprain he sustained on the second-to-last play of the first half in Week 3, both Hendrickson and Lane were listed as full participants. Two-time Pro Bowl center Cam Jurgens, whom they acquired via trade last week, was wearing a red non-contact jersey in his first practice as a Raven, as he remains in the final stages of the concussion protocol, but he remains on track to make his first start this upcoming Sunday.
At 4-1, the Ravens currently sit alone atop the AFC North standings, and with back-to-back games against the Cleveland Browns and Cincinnati Bengals, they're getting key players back and upgrades at important positions for a key juncture in their schedule. If they want to win the division, return to the playoffs after just missing out last year and establish themselves as the cream of the crop in the conference and league as a whole, they'll need to get healthy and hot at the right time.

title: How Hard Are Ravens Pushing Derrick Henry? The Data Is Alarming
full_text:
Ravens rookie offensive coordinator Declan Doyle would not back away from the potential for Derrick Henry to carry the ball 300 times or more this season, despite him being 32-years-old and despite him having never hit that mark in three straight seasons in his Hall of Fame.
Turns out, there was every reason to take him at his word.
Henry is being asked to do, already, things no running back his age has done since the NFL/AFL merger through five weeks of a season, and there is not reason to expect that to change much anytime soon. The Ravens have had to navigate through a new offensive line every week and huge issues at center (including moving rookie guard Vega Ioane there ), and they could very well be without two-time MVP quarterback Lamar Jackson again this week, and it’s been a tough slow on the ground this season in ways Henry never experienced previously in Baltimore, but he is nothing if not a workhorse.
And despite this unprecedented load – as we will detail below – Henry still appeared to be one of the freshest and more impactful players Sunday night as the Ravens produced a game-winning, seven-minute drive in overtime, with backup Snoop Huntley at QB, during which Henry went over 100 yards and had the ball in his hands 25 more times and was at his best putting the game away.
“Obviously, we wanted to score, but I think having that drive was great for us to be able to keep the momentum going, keep the drive going, letting the clock run down, and just keeping that energy,” Henry said after the gutsy win. “I feel like guys were just focused on another level, and  great execution by every single body on offense. The O-line - hell of a job. They did a great job in the run game."
Henry is not having his most explosive season, and he is getting hit behind the line of scrimmage more than ever before as a Raven as part of the experimentation up front, but he remains as integral as ever to this offense and to keep a defense suffering from its share of issues off the field . And no Ravens coach has ever ridden him harder through the first five weeks of a season. And perhaps he could use more help from a blocking standpoint , too).
What he’s taking on already is simply historic.
Henry’s 113 carries through the first five games are the most in NFL history by a running back in his age 32 season. The great Walter Payton is second at 110, Curtis Martin has 105 at this point in that season and Otis Anderson (98) and Emmitt Smith (87) are the only others to carry the ball more than 80 times at that age at this point in the season.
Henry leads them with seven touchdowns through five weeks, while his 4.2 yards/carry is basically league average (Payton was at 4.6 at this point, while Ricky Williams, the only age 32 back since the merger to average over. 4.5/carry in that season, had run just 61 times through Week 5 (but at a robust 5.2/carry). We studied 55 years of age 32 running back data this offseason and the general portrait it painted was quite bleak – but Henry has long been a unicorn and if he gets more consistent run blocking there is reason to believe some of his efficiencies could spike.
Henry’s 476 yards are 30 behind “Sweetness” – the Bears legend who proved incredibly durable and consistent – for the most ever by an age 32 RB through five weeks. When Doyle refused to back away from lofty projection in terms of touches for Henry, he was not foolin around .
“He is a special talent,” Doyle said of Henry this summer. “There are not many guys in the league who can do what he does. The vision for him in the offense is an immense role. Obviously, I don't want to put a number on the amount of [carries], because obviously, as you look at every single week, every week is different. You want to be able to deploy things in different ways, and at the same point in time, he's going to have a pretty large workload.”
Only once previously in his career has Henry run the ball this much through the first five games, and that was in 2001 in Tennessee (142). Think about how the Titans ran their offense through him, and only once did he eclipse this 113 carry mark this soon.
Last year, Henry had just 64 rushes at this point in the season, and the year before he had 95. He’s essentially played one more game to this point than either of those two years at mid-October. In those seasons he was averaging 5.0 and 6.0 per carry to this point, so the yards have been tougher to come by now (0.99 yards before contact this season, 1.77 at this point last year and 2.66 in 2024).
Henry also already has eight catches for 62 yards and a touchdown; he’s never had more than 15 catches in a season as a Raven.
So, um, what exactly would it look like if Henry maintained this pace for the full season? Well, it would be painful, that’s for sure.
He is averaging 22.6 rushes per game, with would yield 384 carries if he kept it up. I did mention he’s never run 300 times in three straight years didn’t I? The 384 carries would surpass anything he’s ever done before. That 2021 season – the only time with more carries through five weeks – was cut short due to injury and he only played eight games.
Henry’s never carried more than 325 in a season in Baltimore and 378 is his career high (2000), the year he went over 2000 rushing yards. Perhaps that will truly be put to the test.

title: Bills' Final Week 6 Injury Report: DJ Moore, Four Others Questionable to Face Raiders
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills have ruled five players as questionable to face the Las Vegas Raiders in Week 6.
After wrapping up practice at UC Irvine on Friday, the Bills issued their final injury report prior to the October 18 road game.
Wide receivers DJ Moore and Josh Palmer, defensive linemen Ed Oliver and TJ Sanders along with slot cornerback Dee Alford are all uncertain to dress on Sunday. The other 10 players listed are all cleared to face the Raiders for the 4:25 p.m. ET kickoff.
One of the 10 without a game designation is starting right tackle Spencer Brown, who left the Week 5 win , and did not return, after 16 snaps due to a back flare-up.
Brown practiced in a limited capacity on Wednesday before improving to full participation on Thursday and Friday. With a  minor "muscle freak out" now in the rearview, the starting right tackle is ready for his 79th regular season appearance in a Bills' uniform.
"Just tweaked it. Nothing major. Disc looks fine. Had an MRI. Looks better than it did last year. Long-term wise that's good to hear," said Brown after Wednesday's practice at UC Irvine.
In another positive development, running back Ty Johnson, who was limited by a hamstring at the first two practices, participated in full on Friday, and he's been cleared for the Sunday game.
Moore and Oliver both sat out the October 12 win over the Los Angeles Rams after injury incidents knocked them out of the October 4 loss to the New England Patriots.
Neither player participated at practice on Wednesday and Thursday, but both returned to the field in a limited capacity on Friday, providing a glimmer of hope that they'll be available for kickoff.
"They've been doing a lot on the side. They've been doing all the walkthroughs and everything. It was good to get them out here today, and just being able to move around," said Bills' head coach Joe Brady . "We'll see how they field coming off the field. Look at it on tape. See what it looked like and have discussions. I say it every week, if they're ready to go, they're gonna play."
Moore sprained his AC joint when hitting the ground during the Week 2 win over the Detroit Lions. He was active in Weeks 3 and 4, but reaggravated the injury against the Patriots. Missing his first game since December 2020, it's likely Moore is itching to play in some capacity on Sunday.
Oliver took a hit to the knee area at the end of a play near the sideline in Week 4. Although it appears to be only a minor injury, the Bills may exercise caution by sitting him again with a Week 7 bye waiting on the other side.
After being scratched in Week 5, Alford and Palmer logged limited participation all three days this week. The former is nursing a minor ankle issue that emerged against the Patriots. The latter is fighting through a shoulder injury from an October 9 practice.
Both Alford and Palmer showed positive signs throughout the week, looking ready to return to game action, by multiple accounts, during media-viewing portions of practice.
Sanders, who has already dealt with a knee issue and a subsequent bout with appendicitis, made his season debut on October 12. He performed well over 51 defensive snaps, but apparently came out of the overtime win bothered by a shoulder. He progressed to full participation at Friday's practice, but remains questionable to play.

title: Five Key Things to Know About Bills vs. Raiders in Week 6
full_text:
When last we saw the Buffalo Bills, it took more than four quarters for Joe Brady’s club to outlast the Los Angeles Rams, 37-34, at SoFi Stadium this past Monday night.
From a long evening to a long afternoon. Last Sunday, the Las Vegas Raiders were in Foxborough to battle the defending AFC champions. The New England Patriots scored early and often and Klint Kubiak’s squad was on the wrong end of a 45-17 blowout.
The Raiders have dropped consecutive games to the Chiefs and Patriots after a 3-0 start. Meanwhile, Josh Allen and company look to maintain their one-game lead in the AFC East with their third road victory in six weeks.
This is another one of those original AFL series that dates back to 1960. And when you include the team’s postseason victories in the 1990 AFC title game (51-3) and the ’93 divisional round (29-23), the Bills own a 22-21 lead in the overall standings.
Dating back to 2017, Buffalo has won three consecutive meetings by a combined 102-47 score. The Bills have scored at least 30 points in each of those victories. The clubs’ last meeting took place in 2023, with the Bills coming away with a 38-10 triumph. Meanwhile, the Raiders took it on the chinstrap, 30-23, six years ago the last time they hosted this series.
The team has a new defensive coordinator this season in Jim Leonhard. However, this year’s unit is off to a very shaky start. Brady’s club has already surrendered 141 points (31-plus in 3 games) and 18 offensive touchdowns. During last season’s 4-1 start, Buffalo allowed 113 points and gave up just 13 offensive TDs.
A season ago, the Raiders ranked a respectable 14th in the league in total defense and pass defense in terms of yards allowed. The club gave up 45 offensive TDs while coming up with just 16 takeaways. In five games this season, Las Vegas has already forced 10 turnovers—nine in three wins and one in two losses.
A season ago, Buffalo’s James Cook became the Bills’ first player since Hall of Famer O.J. Simpson in 1976 to lead the NFL in rushing yards. This season, he’s averaging 106.4 yards per game on the ground. But he’s put the ball on the ground four times in five games (2 lost)— much to the chagrin of the team’s head coach.
While Ashton Jeanty has reached the end zone just twice in 2026, both touchdowns via the air, the sixth overall pick in the NFL draft entered Week 6 ranked 10th in the league in total yards from scrimmage (506). Jeanty leads the Raiders in rushing yards (291) and is also second on the club with 22 receptions.

title: Bills' CB Depth Problem Not Going Away, One Practical Non-Trade Solution Remains
full_text:
The personnel shortage was evident last year in the playoffs, and it followed the Buffalo Bills throughout the offseason.
With five regular season games in the books, the problem persists, and ignoring it won't make it to disappear.
The Bills kept only three true outside cornerbacks on their 53-man roster, and two of them had a combined 11 appearances entering the season.
Essentially, Buffalo is one injury away from being undermanned at the position as was the case when starter Christian Benford was forced to sit out the Week 4 loss to the New England Patriots due to a minor toe issue.
While Benford is back in action, another question has emerged at the other starting spot as Maxwell Hairston, a 2025 first-round pick, has struggled early and often .
Second-round rookie Davison Igbinosun flashed enough potential to earn his first career start in Week 5, but the Bills still have no real depth behind him.
Buffalo's lack of depth extends into the slot, too. On October 12 against the Los Angeles Rams, the Bills was without starting slot cornerback Dee Alford while backup nickel Jordan Hancock remains on Injured Reserve. The lack of bodies caused the team to temporarily sign practice squad defensive back Anthony Kendall to the active roster and deploy him for 31 defensive snaps against Matthew Stafford and Co. on Monday Night Football.
Whether it requires bumping an extra edge rusher off the roster, and onto the practice squad, the Bills would be smart to add a cornerback from the outside during their Week 7 bye.
He may not be the ideal scheme fit, but he's a consummate professional with an All-Pro past who proved he still has some tread left on the tires.
With the Bills clearly shorthanded at cornerback, why have they not re-signed veteran free agent Tre'Davious White ?
"You saw the depth of our corners tested last year through injury. You want to make sure as the season goes along, if injury strikes, that you got enough guys, even if they're not starters," said Bills' general manager Brandon Beane this past spring .
Is it money? Is White not willing to play for under $5 million this season?
Does defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard not see any value in bringing the 31-year-old White into the mix?
It was Beane who said "you would never close the door on bringing a guy like Tre back to Buffalo" back in April.
Since then, the Bills drafted Igbinosun, but they never fully addressed depth. At this point in the season, White is likely the best available option to pursue. Bringing in any other decent player would seemingly require a trade.
At the least, White would provide mentorship for Hairston and Igbinosun to go along with a positive locker room presence. At the most, he'll create a victory-clinching  interception by tipping a Trevor Lawrence pass into Cole Bishop's hands in the playoffs.
White made 16 regular season starts for the Bills last year, totaling 40 tackles, 6.0 TFL, one interception and nine pass break-ups.
Just make the call, Beane.

title: Three Bold Predictions For Buffalo Bills vs. Las Vegas Raiders in Week 6
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills are in the midst of a two-game road trip which began with a Monday Night Football matchup with the Los Angeles Rams. Following their overtime win , the Bills stayed out west as they preparred to take on the Las Vegas Raiders at Allegiant Stadium.
With a record of 4-1, the Bills are still in first place in their division but need to keep winning with the New England Patriots on their heels . This is a game where they will be heavily-favored, but that doesn't always mean success.
Buffalo needs to remain focused to avoid a trap game and leave Las Vegas with a win. Securing that win would be more likely if they make good on the following three bold predictions.
James Cook has had a very strong season statistically.
He enters Week 6 with 532 yards and five touchdowns on the ground, while averaging 5.6 yards per attempt. He's been a focal point of the Bills offense, but has had one major issue. Through five games, Cook already has four fumbles, including one in overtime against the Rams that nearly cost them the game.
Head coach Joe Brady recently said that Cook has to get this issue under control , which should light a fire under the running back's feet. In this bold prediction, that's what happens as Cook tops 100 yards rushing, while also holding onto the ball without fumbling.
2025 first-round pick Maxwell Hairston has struggled mightily this season, even find ing himself benched recently in favor of rookie second-round pick Davison Igbinosun.
While the Ohio State defensive back product hasn't lit the world on fire, he has shown flashes of being a potential playmaker. In this second bold prediction, Igbinosun has his best game as a pro, even recording his first career interception.
Keon Coleman entered this year with the dreaded draft bust label and there were endless calls for the Bills to move on. After five games, he's been able to change the narrative as he's put together a strong start to the season.
Coleman is third on the team with 15 receptions for 224 yards and two touchdowns.
He might not be the WR1 that he was expected to be when selected in 2024, but Coleman has become a reliable part of the offense. In this final bold prediction, he takes advantage of a struggling Raiders defense and records two touchdown receptions.

title: Buffalo Bills vs. Las Vegas Raiders Week 6 Expert Pick Roundup
full_text:
Following a thrilling overtime win on the road against the Los Angeles Rams , the Buffalo Bills decided to stay out west for the week as they prepare to take on the Las Vegas Raiders on the road. The Raiders enter this game with a surprising record of 3-2 while Buffalo is 4-1.
The Raiders are also trying to figure out the right move at quarterback as Kirk Cousins has been starting, but they will eventually turn to No. 1 overall pick Fernando Mendoza. The Bills are at a completely different point as they're trying to get to the Super Bowl during Josh Allen's prime .
There's plenty of intrigue in this one, but who do the experts believe will walk out with the win? Let's check out some of the top media outlets to see who is favored.
Boby Kownack gave his reason for selecting the Bills, saying the Raiders have been better than expected, but doesn't believe they can hang with Buffalo. The main reasons for that include Josh Allen and James Cook.
"There’s also the superman factor: Josh Allen hasn’t been stellar through the air for several weeks now, but he simply finds ways to win, having rushed for 239 yards and a league-leading eight touchdowns. His 5.6 yards-per-carry average is tied for fourth in the league with his teammate James Cook, who is similarly liable to shred a feeble Raiders run defense that hasn’t held a team under 120 yards on the ground since Week 1," Kownack wrote.
Gary Davenport said there's some upset potential, which is always true in the NFL. Still, he believes the Buffalo offense can do enough to win this game, even though there are legitimate concerns defensively.
"Despite concerns about its receiving corps, Buffalo's potent offense should prevent the Raiders from pulling off an upset," Davenport wrote.
It's important to note in this one that these picks are against the spread. That means even though Dave Richard and Jamey Eisenberg selected the Raiders, they are still saying they should do well enough to keep the game closer than the odds suggest.
The experts are mostly in agreement that Buffalo is going to come away with the win, with all but three picks going in their favor.
Las Vegas has been better than expected this season, entering Week 6 with a record of 3-2. That said, their wins are against the Miami Dolphins, Los Angeles Chargers, and New Orleans Saints. Their losses were to the Kansas City Chiefs and New England Patriots. They're also struggling on defense, which is a terrible thing for anyone set to face Buffalo.

title: Buffalo Bills Projected to Be Major Players at NFL Trade Deadline
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills are in yet another season in which expectations are high and it is Super Bowl or bust for Josh Allen and Co.
Knowing that, general manager Brandon Beane must stop at nothing to improve his team before the NFL trade deadline.
And one analyst believes Beane will do just that. Bleacher Report's Kristopher Knox has Buffalo listed among the team's he believes will be the most aggressive before the Nov. 10 trade deadline.
"The Buffalo Bills have looked like one of the top contenders in the AFC through five weeks, though they certainly don't have a flawless roster," Knox said.
"Their defense ranks 30th in yards allowed, and injuries to players like Ed Oliver and Dee Alford haven't helped matters," Knox added.
Beane has been known for his in-season trades during his tenure. In fact, since 2021, Beane has only failed to make an in-season trade once, which came last season.
The problem, as Knox points out, is that the Bills don't have much financial wiggle room to make moves. Over The Cap has the Bills sitting with just $4.8 million in cap space entering Week 6.
That means Buffalo will have to restructure contracts if it wants to do anything substantial, or simply target low-cost players.
Ideally, the Bills throw caution to the wind and take for former approach as the clock continues to tick on the Josh Allen era.
The Bills have one of the worst defenses in the NFL, as evidenced by their ranking 30th in total yards, 31st in passing yards and 28th in points, so all of their biggest needs come on that side of the ball.
While head coach Joe Brady might disagree, the play from the linebacker spot has not been up to snuff this season and an addition at that position is needed.
Cornerback is another sore spot in Buffalo. Christian Benford has been a disappointment, but he is not the biggest issue. Maxwell Hairston hasn't made enough progress and it's clear Davison Igbinosun needs more time to develop.
Sticking with the secondary, we'd love to see an addition at safety, a position that has been an issue for years now because Beane just hasn't been able to figure things out there.
Buffalo may also want to explore adding at wide receiver.
DJ Moore continues to be banged-up and it appears he might have to manage his ailing shoulder all season long, which may impact his play and leaves him at risk of a more serious injury.
Maybe Keon Coleman keeps up his improved play through the season, but we cannot bet on that yet and Joshua Palmer has three catches in four games. The Bills are a significant Moore injury away from being in a precarious spot.
Of course, the Bills won't be able to address all of those positions, but Beane should be moving mountains in order to adequately fill as many of them as possible.

title: Bills' Fourth-Round Rookie LB's Playing Time Will Increase If Joe Brady Has His Way
full_text:
He had the chance to compete for a starting job during training camp , but the rookie apparently wasn't quite yet ready.
After being drafted in April, Buffalo Bills ' fourth-round linebacker Kaleb Elarms-Orr battled returnee Dorian Williams for starting inside linebacker duties alongside co-captain Terrel Bernard.
Elarms-Orr impressed at OTAs , but the ultimate test wouldn't come until the pads came on.
"I think Kaleb had a good spring. It's t-shirts and shorts," said Bills' general manager Brandon Beane.
Although Elarms-Orr subsequently generated buzz for his playmaking during open training camp practices, he seemingly failed to stand out in live preseason game action, and it became apparent the No. 126 overall draft pick needed more time to acclimate himself to the mental and physical speed of NFL action.
With five regular season appearances in the books, however, Elarms-Orr is arguably ready for a more significant role on defense.
"I like where the linebackers are at right now. They're continuing to get better. I'd love for Kaleb to play a little more than he played the other day," said Brady. "That's not an indictment on Dorian [Williams] or TB [Terrel Bernard] that's just being able to get these guys fresh throughout games and when the game's on the line."
Elarms-Orr, who has been on the field only 14 percent of the time thus far, saw seven defensive snaps in the Week 5 primetime win over the Los Angeles Rams. He notably broke up a pass to Puka Nacua on a 2nd-and-10 play late in the second quarter.
Although Brady would publicly disagree , there's a perception that the Bills aren't getting enough production from their inside linebackers as the defense ranks 30th overall (388.6) on the circuit.
As such, there's a case to be made that Elarms-Orr, despite his lack of experience, would be a better alternative to Williams, especially against the pass.
Williams, a 2023 third-round pick , has already permitted two touchdowns in coverage. When targeting the linebacker, opposing passers have an 83.3 completion percentage and a 139.2 quarterback rating.
We suggested that the Bills sign veteran Shaq Thompson off the practice squad to replace Williams in the starting lineup as soon as this week against the Las Vegas Raiders.
If Buffalo isn't comfortable going in that direction for some reason, there's the option of giving more snaps to Elarms-Orr.
The Bills already know what Williams, who has 27 career starts, can do. Now, it's time to find out what the rookie brings to the table, and it sounds like Brady is on board.

title: Jim Leonhard Says 'Some Changes' Being Made to Bills' Defense
full_text:
Entering Week 6, the teams with the 10 worst defenses statistically in the National Football League in terms of yards allowed per game have surrendered an average of 376.84 yards per contest.
And, at the current moment, those same teams have a combined record of 21-27-1.
Furthermore, regarding points allowed per matchup?
Well, so far, on average those squads have given up 28.44 points per game while maintaining a mark of 19-29-1.
Undoubtedly, it’s been a scary sight to see for fans, players, and coaches of those franchises as, fittingly, just three teams from each of those aforementioned groups hold a winning record with the NFL calendar turning closer toward Halloween.
What doesn’t seem to fit, however, is the team that is smack dab in the middle—or even lower—of those two dreadful data points: the Buffalo Bills ( 4-1 OVR, 0-1 AFCE ) .
Right now, the team is ranked 30th in YPG (yards per game) at 388.6 and 28th in points allowed at 28.2 PPG (points per game).
And, that’s not even to mention the Bills’ porous pass defense , which is ranked 31st in the league right now according to FOX Sports after allowing 280.4 YPG to opposing quarterbacks through the first five games.
Simply stated, it’s been BAD .
And, the unit’s only redeeming quality is seemingly the solid contributions of individual players like DeWayne Carter , Deone Walker , and Gregory Rousseau up front, as well as the team’s 15th-ranked rush defense.
However, despite sitting in the middle of the pack in that area, the unit is still giving up 108.2 YPG on the ground, so it’s not as if they’re as dominant as some people might think compared to the rest of the league.
“We’re living in some bad company as far as the success of what we’re doing,” Bills’ first-year defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard said to reporters on Tuesday.
“The reality is we’re one out of five, right? As far as showing up (on defense), and executing a gameplan very well, and finishing a game. So, that’s not good in any sport. . . . We’ve got to make some changes, for sure.
“I’ve got a lot of faith in coaches—and the players—that we’re going to make the adjustments needed to go (forward).”
Once thought to be a savior for all of Buffalo’s previous defensive woes under former longtime Bills’ head coach Sean McDermott over the past nine years, Leonhard’s unit has been downright awful to start the 2026 season.
There’s just no other way to put it, and anyone who tries to defend the continuous struggles of the defensive unit are simply attempting to sugarcoat the awful taste that’s been left in their mouths thus far through five weeks.
Yes, the current leader in the AFC East clubhouse is finding a way to win games behind quarterback Josh Allen and the high-powered offense, but that won’t always be the case . . . especially come playoff time.
If the Bills are going to somehow find their way back to SoFi Stadium later on in February for Super Bowl LXI, which is a trajectory that quarterback Josh Allen’s current stats seems to be putting the team on, then the defensive side is going to have to pull its weight a lot more.
It’s exactly what has held Buffalo back in the past with Allen in January.
And, the team’s new defensive coordinator isn’t naive to that glaring fact. Leonhard knows that the product that’s been displayed on the field by his players isn’t good enough, and it needs to start changing in a hurry.
“It’s time to start being good at something, right? I mean . . . that’s our struggles right now. It’s too inconsistent to pretend that we’re building, and working, and making improvements.
“Like, everything’s being evaluated right now—starting with every decision I’m making—and we’ve got to put (the players) in better positions to have success, (and) guys have to make plays when given opportunities,” Leonhard continued.
“This is professional football. If we don’t feel like the answers are there, well then—year—there gets to be some big conversations. But, first things first, we’ve got to fix it with what we have and the players that we’re playing with on Sundays, and who we’re gameplanning for.
“Like, we’ve got to find a way to give them gameplans that we can go out there and execute.”
Last week, rookie cornerback Davison “IGB” Igbinosun received the starting nod on the boundary opposite Christian Benford over 2025 first-round pick Maxwell Hairston, who struggled mightily in Week 4 against the New England Patriots .
Now, it seems more changes could be on the way.
After allowing 454 total yards and 34 points in front of the nation on Monday Night Football to the Los Angeles Rams—a team previously only scoring 21.25 PPG heading into the matchup—Leonhard’s next opportunity to change the narrative will be on the road against the Las Vegas Raiders at Allegiant Stadium for a 4:25 p.m. ET kickoff.

title: Bills Given Two Intriguing Safety Trade Targets to Fix Secondary
full_text:
Entering Week 6, the Buffalo Bills have an impressive 4-1 record , but that doesn't mean they are without flaws. While they're the No. 1 scoring offense with 164 points in five games, the Buffalo defense has been a problem .
The Bills are currently ranked 28th in points surrendered with 141 and 30th in yardage, giving up 1,943. Their biggest concern comes in the passing game, with Buffalo giving up 1,402 passing yards, which is 31st in the league.
These struggles have Ryan Talbot of Syracuse.com urging Brandon Beane to get on the phones and find an available safety. He has two elite playmakers in mind, saying they should call the Arizona Cardinals about Budda Baker or the Los Angeles Chargers about Derwin James.
"Listen, if I'm Brandon Beane, I'm working the phones. Hello, Arizona Cardinals? Budda Baker, is he available? Chargers? What about Derwin James?" Talbot said.
"I'm looking for safety help. I'm looking for anything I can get at that position. It's bare bones there, it's not great. You can hope for Jordan Hancock to come off the IR here at some point, maybe he can be part of the answer."
Arizona is sitting at 1-4 and just traded away wide receiver Marvin Harrison Jr. There's a belief that they could be ready to host a fire sale and load up on draft picks for a roster overhaul. Baker would be an intriguing target, and despite turning 30 in January, he's still playing at a highe level. Through five games, Baker has 36 tackles, two sacks, three pass breakups, and one interception.
Baker has a cap hit of $19.216 million this season and $20.891 million in 2027.
The Chargers are in worse shape, with a record of 0-5. They haven't signalled that they're ready to start making moves, but James is someone who could bring back a decent draft pick. He is also 30 years old, meaning he wouldn't be part of a rebuild (should the Chargers be interested in one), but could help a team such as Buffalo looking for a title.
James has played in three games this season and has 21 tackles and one pass breakup. The Chargers still might not be willing to move him after signing James to a three-year extension worth $75.6 million this offseason.
Even if it's not Baker or James, the Bills need to find help in their secondary. They also shouldn't limit their search to safeties, since their cornerback corps has been an issue as well.

title: Bills' Week 6 Injury Report: Spencer Brown Upgraded, No progress for DJ Moore
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills ' second Week 6 injury report looks almost identical to the first with one notable difference.
Of the 15 players listed, only one accounted for a status change, and it was a welcome one. Starting right tackle Spencer Brown was upgraded to full participation at Thursday's practice after being limited during Wednesday's walkthrough.
A back flare-up forced Brown out of the October 12 road win over the Los Angeles Rams after only 16 offensive snaps . Backup Tylan Grable came in to finish the game, but he likely won't be needed to start against the Las Vegas Raiders on October 18.
"Just tweaked it. Nothing major. Disc looks fine. Had an MRI. Looks better than it did last year. Long-term wise that's good to hear. It's [current issue] straight up just muscular freaking out," said Brown on Wednesday .
On Thursday, Brown confirmed to reporters that he was good to go for Sunday's game.
For the second day in a row , wide receiver DJ Moore and defensive lineman Ed Oliver did not practice.
Moore, who was wearing a red non-contact jersey, spent the media-viewing portion of practice on the sidelines. Oliver was seen doing exercises with a trainer off to the side.
Both players missed Monday's game due to injury issues that emerged during the October 4 loss to the New England Patriots. Moore reaggravated his ACL joint sprain while Oliver took a hit to the knee. Neither returned after leaving the field under their own power.
Moore initially injured his shoulder during the Week 2 win over the Detroit Lions. He played in Weeks 3 and 4 before sitting out in Week 5. It was his first missed game since December 2020.
Oliver had a knee scope during the offseason, but it's unknown if this current issue is connected. He also missed the Week 2 victory due to a hip flexor.
At this point, one has to wonder if the Bills don't just play it safe and sit both players with the Week 7 bye to follow.
Ed Oliver, Tyrell Shavers, and Zane Durant off to the side with an athletic trainer. pic.twitter.com/u6OoAgkm6e
Neither wide receiver Josh Palmer and slot cornerback Dee Alford were available for Monday Night Football, but both appear on the cusp of returning to game action against the Raiders.
Palmer injured his shoulder during last Friday's practice. He was a limited participant on Wednesday and Thursday, wearing a red non-contact jersey. Based upon a post-practice conversation , Buffalo News' reporter Jay Skurski surmises that Palmer will suit up on Sunday .
Alford tweaked his ankle against the Patriots, but appeared to move well at Thursday's practice. He was officially limited, but seems to be trending toward a Week 6 return.
Defensive tackle TJ Sanders and running back Ty Johnson practiced on a limited basis for the second day in a row after getting nicked up on Monday.
Sanders, who had been slowed by a knee issue followed by a bout with appendicitis, made his season debut in Week 5. He seemingly made it through the game intact, but popped up on the injury report with a shoulder.
Meanwhile, Johnson apparently tweaked his hamstring. Considering a hamstring injury kept him out for almost all of August into September , this is one to monitor.

title: Panthers-Eagles Suddenly Means Something — These 3 Matchups Could Decide It
full_text:
This isn't exactly where most people expected the Carolina Panthers to be heading into Week 6.
Carolina is 2-2, coming off a bye and heading to Philadelphia with a chance to put itself right in the middle of the early NFC playoff conversation. The Eagles are only 2-3 and have lost three straight, so this game looks a whole lot different than it did when the schedule came out.
Then Thursday changed things even more.
Jalen Hurts was ruled out with a superficial blood clot, meaning Tanner McKee will get the start for Philadelphia. That obviously helps Carolina, but I'm not ready to act like this suddenly becomes an easy road win.
The Eagles still have plenty of talent, and Carolina hasn't exactly reached the point where we should expect them to walk into Philadelphia and win. If the Panthers are going to come home 3-2, these are the three matchups I think will have the biggest say in whether it happens.
Let's start with Young because, at this point, how could we not?
He's playing the best football of his career, throwing for 1,268 yards and nine touchdowns through four games. He hasn't thrown for fewer than 287 yards in a game this season, and Carolina is averaging more than 30 points per game.
I've spent the last few weeks trying to figure out what's really changed for Young this season . Whatever the answer is, he looks more comfortable in this offense than he has at any point since Carolina drafted him.
Philadelphia should give us another pretty good idea of where Young is right now. According to the Panthers' preview of the Eagles , Philadelphia has allowed 222 passing yards per game. The Eagles don't blitz a ton, but they've still been able to generate pressure with four rushers on 32% of their opponents' dropbacks.
That's the part I'll be watching.
Young has looked comfortable in this offense and has done a much better job of taking care of the football. But if Philadelphia can get pressure without having to send extra guys, things could get a little tougher.
If Young gets time, though, I like Carolina's chances of moving the football. Tetairoa McMillan is coming off a 192-yard game, Jalen Coker is back, and Darren Waller can't be overlooked.
That's a lot more for a defense to worry about than Carolina had around Young earlier in his career.
If there's one guy on Philadelphia's defense who worries me, it's Jalen Carter.
Carter already has three sacks through five games, matching his total from all of last season. He also had two strip-sacks against Jacksonville last week, and he's one of those guys who can completely screw up what an offense wants to do if you let him get going.
Carolina can't let that happen.
That's easier said than done when Young has already been pressured on nearly half of his dropbacks this season. He's handled it better than anyone could've expected, but asking him to keep surviving that kind of pressure every week probably isn't the best plan.
There is some good news up front. Taylor Moton was a full participant in Thursday's practice as he works his way back, although rookie right tackle Monroe Freeling remained out with a knee injury.
Carter is still going to put plenty of pressure on the middle of Carolina's offensive line. This is where Robert Hunt and the rest of that group have to make sure Young isn't spending the afternoon with Carter in his face.
It matters for Chuba Hubbard, too.
Hubbard finally got going against Detroit with 122 yards and two touchdowns. If Carolina can keep Carter out of the backfield, it gives Hubbard a chance to build on that game and keeps the Panthers from putting everything on Young.
Nobody is going to completely erase Carter for four quarters. Carolina just can't let him take over the game.
This matchup became a whole lot more interesting Thursday afternoon.
The Panthers spent most of the week preparing for Hurts before learning that McKee will start Sunday . He hasn't played this season, but this isn't his first time on an NFL field. McKee has appeared in six games with two starts, throwing for 597 yards, five touchdowns and only one interception.
So no, I'm not looking at this like Carolina automatically gets a win because Hurts isn't playing.
What the Panthers need to do is make McKee beat them. Saquon Barkley has been dealing with a hamstring injury and missed practice Wednesday and Thursday. If he plays, Carolina can't let Philadelphia lean on him all afternoon and make life easy on its backup quarterback.
I'd much rather see McKee staring at third-and-8 than third-and-2.
That's where Derrick Brown and Carolina's defensive front come into this. Philadelphia has gone through plenty of changes up front, and the Panthers have a chance to make McKee uncomfortable if they can slow down the running game and put the Eagles in obvious passing situations.
Carolina's defense has been hard to figure out all season. I recently wrote about how this defense somehow makes absolutely no sense , but we've also seen this group come up with stops when it absolutely had to.
McKee might play well. He's done enough in limited opportunities that Carolina has to respect him, but there's a difference between respecting a backup quarterback and letting him settle into the game.
Make him uncomfortable and see what happens.
I'm not calling a Week 6 game a must-win because that's going way too far. But let's not pretend this isn't a pretty big opportunity for the Panthers.
Before the bye, I wondered whether Carolina's 2-2 record might be lying to us . Philadelphia was the game I wanted to see before deciding just how seriously we should take this team, and I still feel that way.
The Panthers are coming off a bye, Philadelphia has lost three straight and the Eagles will be without their starting quarterback. Carolina has spent the first month of the season making people look at this team a little differently, and going into Philadelphia and winning would only add to that.
It probably comes down to the same things most games do. Protect Young, don't let Philadelphia's best players wreck the afternoon and make the backup quarterback uncomfortable.
Do those three things, and 3-2 would look pretty good heading back to Carolina.

title: Panthers-Eagles Betting Outlook: A Wild Line Swing & 3 Props That Stand Out
full_text:
What a difference a few days can make for the Carolina Panthers. They started the week as underdogs heading into Philadelphia, but then Jalen Hurts was ruled out with a superficial blood clot, and the betting market quickly shifted toward Carolina. Suddenly, the Panthers are getting a level of respect we haven't seen much of lately.
Reuters reported Thursday that Hurts will miss Sunday's game and Tanner McKee is expected to start in his place. I'll admit, watching what happened to the line after that news made me do a double take. But once you get past the initial shock, some of these numbers aren't as crazy as they might look.
Bryce Young has been dealing, Tetairoa McMillan just went off for 192 yards, and Chuba Hubbard finally got rolling against Detroit. So I went through the numbers at DraftKings Sportsbook , and a few immediately caught my attention.
Philadelphia opened as a 1.5-point favorite at DraftKings Sportsbook, but that didn't last. After the Hurts news broke, Sports Illustrated's betting team reported that the line swung five points, moving Carolina all the way to a 3.5-point favorite. The number has continued moving since then, which shows just how much uncertainty Hurts' absence has created around this game.
Do I completely trust Carolina as a road favorite yet? I'm not there, because this is still a 2-2 Panthers team, and Philadelphia still has plenty of talent even without Hurts. The Eagles have dropped three straight, though, while Carolina went into its bye after beating Detroit 32-26.
There's another reason I don't think we can chalk the entire shift up to Hurts being out. Carolina has scored 121 points through four games, the most the franchise has ever scored over the first four games of a season. The Panthers have actually done something to earn some of this respect, and let's be real, we haven't been able to say that very often lately.
Young's passing-yard total is hovering around 240 yards at DraftKings Sportsbook , and this was probably the number that surprised me the most. According to the Panthers' official statistics , he's thrown for 1,268 yards through four games, which comes out to 317 per game. That's a pretty big gap between what Young has actually been producing and the number we're seeing for Sunday.
It gets even more interesting when you look at his game-by-game totals. Young has thrown for 361, 287, 291, and 329 yards, meaning his lowest output of the season is still well above Sunday's number. Four games isn't a huge sample, but he's been remarkably consistent throwing the football so far.
There is something that gives me pause, and that's how this game could unfold with McKee starting instead of Hurts. If Carolina gets ahead early, Dave Canales may not need Young throwing it 35 or 40 times. Still, we've spent years wondering whether Young could consistently push the football downfield, and now we're looking at a number around 240 yards and wondering why it isn't higher.
Hubbard finally looked like Hubbard against Detroit, carrying the ball 20 times for a season-high 122 yards and two touchdowns while averaging 6.1 yards per carry. The Panthers' official stats have him at 306 yards on 61 attempts this season, an even 5.0 yards per carry. His rushing-yard total was listed at 71.5 at DraftKings Sportsbook in Thursday's published odds.
My first reaction was that 72 yards doesn't seem like much after what we just watched against Detroit. Then I went back and looked at Hubbard's first three games, and he didn't reach 70 yards in any of them. That's why this number isn't nearly as simple as it first appears.
I'm not ready to assume one big afternoon suddenly means Carolina's running game is fixed. At the same time, if the Panthers are playing from ahead Sunday, this could turn into exactly the kind of game where Canales keeps feeding Hubbard and tries to shorten things in the second half. Of all the numbers I looked at, this is probably the one I could talk myself into either direction on the easiest.
Good luck figuring out what to expect from McMillan after what he just did to Detroit. He caught 14 passes for 192 yards and two touchdowns, and the Panthers noted in their Inside the Numbers breakdown that he became the first player in franchise history with at least 10 catches, 175 receiving yards and two touchdowns in the same game.
He enters Sunday with 26 catches for 385 yards through four games and is averaging 14.8 yards per reception.
His receiving-yard total was listed at 66.5 at DraftKings Sportsbook in Thursday's published odds. Nobody should expect another 192-yard afternoon every week because that's ridiculous, but 66.5 is a completely different conversation. Young clearly isn't afraid to look his way, and McMillan has already shown he can turn a handful of opportunities into a big afternoon.
What I like about McMillan right now is that Carolina doesn't have to force everything his way. Jalen Coker is back, Darren Waller has become another option for Young, and suddenly defenses have several guys they have to account for. If Carolina continues spreading the ball around, McMillan might actually get some better opportunities instead of seeing his production disappear.
After watching him put up 192 yards, I'm not trying to guess what he's going to do for an encore. I'm more interested in seeing how Philadelphia decides to defend him and whether Young keeps looking his way when the Eagles start adjusting.
That's the question I kept coming back to while looking through all of this. The Panthers went from underdogs to favorites on the road against the Eagles, Young has a passing-yard number that somehow feels low, Hubbard is coming off 122 yards, and we're already wondering what McMillan can possibly do for an encore.
Think about where this franchise was not that long ago, and those are some pretty wild conversations to be having.
I'm not ready to say Carolina has arrived because four games isn't enough for that. Philadelphia also isn't suddenly a pushover because Hurts isn't playing, and McKee has played well enough in limited opportunities that Carolina can't just show up and expect to win. There are still plenty of reasons to be cautious about this matchup.
But there does seem to be something different about this Panthers offense. Maybe it's Young taking another step, maybe it's finally having legitimate weapons around him, or maybe it's simply what happens when a young team starts believing it can score with anybody. Whatever it is, the betting market has noticed too, and now Carolina gets another chance Sunday to show whether that respect is deserved.

title: Bryce Young Isn't the Panthers' Biggest Question Anymore
full_text:
For almost three years, every conversation about the Carolina Panthers eventually came back to the same question: Is Bryce Young good enough?
I've asked it plenty of times myself. After what we watched during his first couple of seasons, I don't think it was an unfair question. Carolina took Young No. 1 overall, and at some point, you needed to start seeing something that made you feel better about that decision.
Four games into this season, I'm starting to wonder if we've been asking the wrong question. Young has thrown for 1,268 yards, nine touchdowns, and only two interceptions. He's thrown for at least 287 yards in every game, Carolina is putting points on the board, and we're no longer spending every Monday trying to figure out what's wrong with the quarterback.
That's a pretty big change from where we were not that long ago. Young has spent most of his career trying to prove he's good enough for the Panthers. Maybe now it's time for the Panthers to show they're good enough to do something with him.
I'm not going to pretend four good games erase everything that happened before this season. They don't, and there's still a lot of football left. But Young is playing really good football right now, and I don't know how else to put it.
We wanted him to push the ball downfield more, and he's doing it. We wanted him to take better care of the football, and he's doing that, too. More than anything, we wanted to see an offense that didn't look like it was scared to put the game in his hands, and we're finally getting that.
It's not like everything around him suddenly became perfect, either. Young has been pressured on nearly half of his dropbacks , and he's still putting up the best numbers of his career. That's probably what has impressed me the most.
For the longest time, I wondered what Young would look like if Carolina just gave him some help. Now Tetairoa McMillan looks like a legitimate No. 1 receiver, Chuba Hubbard is coming off a 122-yard game, Jalen Coker is back, and Darren Waller has been sneakily good. Carolina finally gave Young some guys to work with, and he's making it count.
He just looks more comfortable out there, too. Young talked recently about how much input offensive coordinator Brad Idzik gives him during the week, and I wrote about how different things seem for Young in this offense . Maybe it's the weapons, maybe it's another year in the offense, or maybe Young is simply getting better. It's probably a little bit of all of it.
Whatever the reason, it's working. For most of his career, it felt like Carolina was trying to figure out whether it could win with Young. Now he's becoming one of the biggest reasons they're winning.
That's what makes Sunday in Philadelphia so interesting to me. I'm not saying beating the Eagles suddenly makes Carolina a Super Bowl contender. We're four games into the season, and nobody needs to get carried away yet.
But if you want people to start taking you seriously, these are the games you eventually have to win. Philadelphia has lost three straight, Jalen Hurts is out, and Tanner McKee will start in his place. Carolina is coming off a bye after beating Detroit 32-26, so you couldn't ask for a much better opportunity.
That's really what I want to see from Carolina now. We've spent years talking about patience, development, rebuilding, and waiting to see what Young becomes. Well, we're starting to get our answer, and now the Panthers have to do something with it.
Protect him better. Keep putting weapons around him. Give him a defense that doesn't make him feel like he has to score every time he touches the ball. When you get a chance to go on the road against a struggling team playing without its starting quarterback, take advantage of it.
That's why Sunday feels like a little more than just a chance to get to 3-2. I don't need Young to throw for 350 yards and four touchdowns to convince me he's playing well. He's already spent the first month of the season answering most of the questions I had about him.
Now I want to see what Carolina does with it.
If this version of Young is what we're going to keep seeing, the conversation around the Panthers has to change with him. For years, we kept asking whether Bryce Young was good enough for Carolina.
Maybe it's finally time to find out if Carolina is good enough for Bryce Young.
Mark Livingston is a South Carolina native and recent Penn State graduate with a degree in Digital Media and Journalism.
