title: Tank Dell Injury Update: Where Texans WR Stands for Week 6 vs. Jaguars
full_text:
It's been a little over a week since the Houston Texans first activated the 21-day practice window returning from injured reserve for wide receiver Tank Dell, who hasn't played in an NFL game dating back to when he first suffered his severe knee injury in December of 2024.
But now that Dell is back at practice–– and as of Wednesday's injury report, was able to be a full participant–– the big question for the Texans' wideout is when he'll be able to get back on the field for a game, and whether or not it could be as soon as Week 6 against the Jacksonville Jaguars.
And while Dell's full participation in practice is certainly a great sign for how he's progressing, there's no clear determination just yet on whether he'll be good to play this weekend.
Texans general manager Nick Caserio recently appeared on 95.7 The Fan with Seth Payne and Sean Pendergast heading into their Week 6 game in London, where Caserio dove into the status of Dell and what his availability could look like moving forward.
And overall, Dell seems to be "trending in the right direction." However, there remains no clear determination just yet on when the Texans might be activating him from the injured reserve.
"With those players, you have 21 days. So, he practiced last week. He'll practice again here this week. We'll kind of evaluate where he is. Unless he has a setback––he's trending in the right direction," Caserio said of Dell.
"So, whether it's this week or next week, some of this is going to be like: 'Okay, how does this practice go? What does that look like?' Make sure he's loaded properly, make sure that he's prepared so that when he does go out there and actually play, he's ready to go for that."
Dell has been showing some really positive signs when it comes to getting back to 100%. Returning to practice is a big part of that, and participating in full for multiple sessions will be the next step for his availability to look even more promising moving forward.
But Dell also has two key factors to clear within his recovery and return to practice before he's officially deemed ready to be activated from injured reserve : that's handling contact, and getting back his top-end speed that made him such a potent offensive weapon before his injury.
The longer that Dell is able to get his feet wet in practice and get more comfortable back in pads, the better his chances will be to finally be activated after a nearly two-year wait to return to the field.
However, seeing those aspects of his recovery develop in practice might end up extending his absence an extra one or two weeks before the Texans do activate him from injured reserve, and would thus sideline him for Week 6 against the Jaguars .
What might end up being the most ideal approach for the Texans to take is to wait until their Week 8 bye before activating Dell from injured reserve.
The Wednesday of Houston's bye in Week 8 marks the end of Houston's 21-day window to elevate Dell to the active roster, and doing so then could essentially allow Dell one more full week of practice before their next game in Week 9 against the LA Chargers.
When Caserio was asked about the possibility of waiting until the bye week to activate Dell, he didn't shoot the idea down. But the focus was simply on how this week's practice looks before Week 6. Then the team would re-evaluate from there.
"Look, you have 21 days. So, within that 21-day period, you're either going to activate him, or you're not. So, we'll kind of handle this week, we'll kind of see how this week goes, and make an assessment at the end of the week," Caserio continued.
"But, he's certainly done everything we've asked him to do, and he's turning in the right direction."
The main takeaway from all of this? Dell's moving in the right direction to get back on the field in the coming weeks. As to when his return to the field might be, though, could be anywhere from Week 6 in London, all the way until Week 9 on the road in Los Angeles.

title: Why Texans Must Temper Expectations for Marvin Harrison Jr. vs. Jaguars
full_text:
The Houston Texans will be getting their first look at Marvin Harrison Jr. in his new jersey following his move from the Arizona Cardinals, as head coach DeMeco Ryans confirmed on Wednesday that the team is planning on their new wide receiver being active for Week 6 against the Jacksonville Jaguars.
It's bound to be an exciting moment for Harrison Jr. and everyone watching, as the Texans' newest pass-catcher will be bringing in balls from his college quarterback, C.J. Stroud, once again , and potentially mark the beginning of a fresh start in the NFL with a new situation in Houston.
But when it comes to Harrison Jr.'s chances to make an impact in Week 6 against the Jaguars, just how involved will the Texans' newest receiver be in the overall game plan?
Of course, Harrison Jr. is bound to get on the field for his fair share of plays, but having been in the building for less than a week, there's a good chance that the Texans' newest wideout will be a bit limited in his debut.
Now, in a few weeks' time, Harrison Jr. will slowly find himself as a bigger and more important piece of the Texans' game plan. Houston invested a premium second-round pick for the talent he brings to the table , and will be hungry to squeeze some of that production out of him as soon as this season.
But the turnaround that Harrison Jr. has to face–– going from an entirely new team and offensive system with different plays in a one-week span–– it's hard to expect the Texans' newest wideout to catch onto and adjust the entire playbook in such a short amount of time.
Instead, the Texans will likely take things a bit slower when it comes to Harrison Jr.'s involvement; letting him learn a select number of plays before this weekend's matchup in London, getting him involved in those specific reps, and hoping that he can have a smoother transition as a result.
DeMeco Ryans even addressed the Texans' plans for Harrison Jr. in terms of workload on Wednesday after revealing Houston's new receiver was set to play against the Jaguars, where it was clear he wasn't exactly going to be an every-snap player just yet.
"When you get a player to come in late as Marvin has, like, what is he able to pick up on? We go through the entire playbook, we'll have set plays, and we'll make sure it's as easy as possible for him to get lined up so he can play fast," Ryans said.
"Don't expect him to come out and play all 60 snaps in the game, but we'll make sure he gets what he needs, and make sure he's confident in what we're asking him to do."
While Week 6 against the Jaguars could see Harrison Jr.'s workload on the lighter side, it's only a matter of time before those snaps and opportunities grow larger.

Houston has their bye sitting in Week 8 after facing the New York Giants next weekend, and could set up the right amount of time necessary for the 2024 No. 4 pick to really get an understanding of his new offense.

title: 4 Noteworthy Quotes From Marvin Harrison Jr.'s First Texans Presser
full_text:
The Houston Texans finally got Marvin Harrison Jr. in the building for his first practice with the team on Wednesday, only a few days out from his first game in uniform against the Jacksonville Jaguars in Week 6.
And after that Texans' practice, Harrison Jr. was able to speak to the media for the first time since the deal to ship him out from the Arizona Cardinals went down earlier this weekend.
Let's sort through four of the more notable points to come out of Harrison Jr.'s first presser as a part of the Texans:
One thing Texans fans will notice pretty quickly about Harrison Jr. is that he's a pretty reserved personality.
However, even while not your typical alpha, outspoken NFL wide receiver, he made sure to express the excitement he has in store with his new situation, along with pairing up next to his college quarterback in C.J. Stroud .
"I'm excited to be here," Harrison Jr said. "I'm excited to help this team win games. I'm excited to be with C.J. again, and help C.J. to the best of my abilities."
"Always watched the Texans from afar. Obviously, just watching C.J. So, it's pretty surreal to be able to play with him now again, and just help him out the best I can."
As for Harrison's biggest goals for both now and the future, he kept things pretty simple:
"Help the team win. Period."
While the process for Harrison Jr.'s move out of Arizona was a bit different than your typical trade, it seems Harrison Jr. himself found out Houston was his ultimate destination a little bit before the entire world did–– or at least until DeMeco Ryans made it clear during his post-game presser after beating the Tennessee Titans.
"My agent told me, obviously, before the news broke to you guys," Harrison Jr. said of how he found out about the trade to Houston. "DeMeco kind of did his thing as well. But, yeah, before that."
As to whether or not Houston was the place he wanted to be, he set the record straight that he really had no control over where he would be headed after the Cardinals.
"When you get traded, you don't really have that option, you know?"
Harrison Jr. was also asked about how he felt about some viral clips circling around social media showcasing some of his routes run during his time with the Cardinals: some of which might've not looked the most polished or with 110% effort that you'd expect.
look at the effort on this route from Marvin Harrison Jr. on 2nd and 6 pic.twitter.com/xu6jK6VJwe
However, Harrison Jr. simply brushed off those types of comments or concerns. Simply put, everybody has their own opinion, and he knows the player and person he can be.
"I mean, everybody has their own opinions," Harrison Jr. said. "That's really the best way I can put that. Everybody has their own opinions and what they're going to gather from information."
"I know who I am as a player. I know who I am as a person. However people want to label me or think of me, that's their opinion."
Harrison Jr.'s first team session in the Texans' facility on Wednesday also meant he was able to be coached up by DeMeco Ryans for the first time .
And based on first impressions, Harrison Jr. had one clear takeaway on what Ryan’s brings to the table: energy.
"Energy, man. Energy. That's one thing you can always pinpoint, especially with a defensive guy," Harrison Jr. on what he's noticed about DeMeco Ryans. "They always want to bring the energy. You can kind of see that throughout the whole team, and the energy he brings day in and day out."

title: Colts Could Be Without Key Offensive Weapon Against Titans
full_text:
Friday brought a mixed bag of injury news for the Indianapolis Colts ahead of Sunday's AFC South matchup with the Tennessee Titans.
Several key players appear to be trending in the right direction, but Indianapolis has already ruled out two contributors, and rookie tight end Tyler Warren remains questionable.
Of all the developments on Friday's report, Warren's status is easily the one that concerns me most.
Warren was arguably the only bright spot for this offense in last week's 34-22 loss to Pittsburgh, catching seven passes for 83 yards and adding a one-yard rushing touchdown.
Through five games, he has 30 catches for 213 yards and two touchdowns, trailing only Josh Downs in receiving yards for Indianapolis. Losing him would be a massive blow to a passing attack that is already running out of healthy weapons.
Alec Pierce remains on injured reserve, Darius Slayton was released Friday without ever appearing in a game for Indianapolis, and Dulin has now been ruled out for a second straight week.
That leaves Keenan Allen, Josh Downs, Laquon Treadwell and Deion Burks as the primary wide receiver options, with Warren's status potentially making things even thinner.
Warren wasn't listed on the injury report Wednesday or Thursday, making his late-week appearance with a groin injury even more concerning.
The good news is Allen and Downs have logged two straight full practices after lighter workloads Wednesday. Daniel Jones was also a full participant all three days despite remaining on the report with an ankle designation.
Will Mallory practiced fully all week as he works his way back from a thumb injury, although he is also listed as questionable while Indianapolis decides whether to activate him from injured reserve.
Outside of Warren, Carlies and Dulin, Friday was fairly encouraging.
Jonathan Taylor logged his second consecutive full practice, while Jalen Travis progressed from not practicing Wednesday to limited Thursday and full participation Friday.
Grover Stewart returned to full participation after a rest day Thursday, while Charvarius Ward has now practiced fully on back-to-back days. DeForest Buckner did not practice Friday, but his absence was rest-related.
Carlies being out for a second straight week still hurts a linebacker room that has struggled early this season, but Warren's status carries the biggest offensive implications.
Tennessee owns PFF's 26th-ranked coverage unit through five weeks, which should give Indianapolis an opportunity to attack through the air.
But without Pierce, Dulin and potentially Warren, I am not sure the Colts have enough firepower to fully take advantage. That could put even more pressure on Downs and Taylor.
Tennessee ranks eighth in both PFF run-defense grade and tackling grade, meaning the matchup on the ground may be tougher than its 0-5 record suggests.
With Indianapolis' bottom ranked pass defense, both teams may want to attack through the air.
With an already depleted receiving corps, having Warren available could be the difference between an offense that finds its rhythm and another frustrating afternoon for Daniel Jones.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: 3 Most Important Things Colts’ Shane Steichen Said Ahead of Week 6
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts will look to get back to .500 on Sunday when they host the Tennessee Titans in an AFC South matchup. Indianapolis has several areas to clean up as it looks to maintain its position in the division and continue building toward its goals.
Ahead of the game, head coach Shane Steichen addressed the media to discuss the team's preparation and what the Colts need to do to put together a complete performance against Tennessee. Here are three of the most important takeaways from his comments.
The Colts have received inconsistent production from their wide receivers in recent weeks, and opposing defenses are beginning to adjust to their most productive targets. Heading into Sunday's matchup with the Titans, head coach Shane Steichen knows the offense must find ways to counter those adjustments.
One challenge has been getting Josh Downs involved when defenses focus on taking him away, particularly on third downs. Steichen acknowledged the attention Downs has received and explained how Indianapolis hopes to respond.
“Yeah I mean, each and every week we’ve got to be prepared for what defenses do to him," Steichen said. "They're doubling him on third down a few times...we’ve got to do a great job of moving him around to get him freed up when teams are doing that because he is a hell of a player."
When defenses take away the first option, Steichen said the Colts must capitalize on opportunities elsewhere in the passing game, saying they're always looking for new ways to get their playmakers the ball.
Indianapolis could also have another option as it looks for more production from its receivers. The Colts recently added Quez Watkins, who could provide a vertical threat if he earns a role against Tennessee. Steichen was noncommittal about whether Watkins would make his debut this week.
Steichen identified turnovers as a major area of emphasis for the Colts heading into Sunday's matchup with the Titans. Indianapolis is -6 in turnover differential, tied for worst in the league.
Steichen said this week that taking the ball away, as well as protecting it, were the main points of emphasis in this week's preparation for Tennessee.
“Obviously, you got – you preach it, but you got to practice it like crazy," he said. "It's got to be all day, every day in practice. You can't talk about it. You got to go do it.”
The message is clear: Indianapolis has to improve on both sides of the turnover equation.
With the AFC South matchup approaching, the Colts will look to turn that emphasis in practice into results on Sunday. As Steichen made clear, stressing the importance of turnovers is not enough. Indianapolis must execute when it matters.
Jonathan Taylor has remained a productive part of the Colts' offense, but Indianapolis has yet to create the explosive runs that have made Taylor so dangerous throughout his career. Ahead of Sunday's matchup with the Titans, Steichen acknowledged that getting those game-changing plays back into the offense is an area the team needs to address.
“Obviously, the chunk plays like we saw last year, we haven't had those in the run game, and it'd be great to get back to that and get those explosives going forward,” Steichen said.
Steichen pointed to both scheme and execution as factors in creating more opportunities for Taylor, who hasn't recorded a run of 25 yards or more in over 570 snaps. Indianapolis has to adjust to the defensive fronts it faces each week while making sure its players execute when the offense gets the looks it wants.
“Execution's got to be at a premium.," Steichen said.
Taylor's ability to turn routine carries into explosive gains can add another dimension to the Colts' offense. Against Tennessee, Indianapolis will look to create the conditions for those bigger plays and give its star running back more opportunities to break through.

title: Colts Pull Plug on Darius Slayton Experiment: Is a Corresponding Move Coming?
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts have released wide receiver Darius Slayton, the team announced, ending a bizarre month-long stint with the team.
We have released WR Darius Slayton.
The Colts signed Slayton on Sept. 22 in an attempt to remedy their injury problems. The idea was that Slayton would reconnect with a former teammate Daniel Jones to help stabilize the passing game until the Colts returned to full strength.
Less than a month later, Slayton is out of Indianapolis without having appeared in any of the four games he was available for.
Indianapolis caught the injury bug early in the season at wide receiver. Alec Pierce suffered an ankle injury in Week 2, Ashton Dulin has been navigating a hamstring injury and Keenan Allen has dealt with a few bumps and bruises, missing the game in London.
Pierce’s absence left a huge void in the Colts passing game, taking away their best field-stretching deep threat. He had established himself as one of the NFL's most productive downfield receivers, leading the league in yards per reception in both 2024 and 2025. With Pierce expected to miss several weeks and Dulin also dealing with an injury, the Colts needed another option capable of stretching the field.
Slayton offered a potential solution to both problems. The seven-year veteran averaged 15.0 yards per catch across his time with the New York Giants and already had an established connection with Daniel Jones, having played alongside the quarterback for six seasons. Indianapolis was betting that chemistry and Slayton's downfield ability could help keep the passing game afloat until Pierce returned.
The move made sense on paper, but the Colts never got to see whether Slayton could deliver. He was inactive for his first two games with Indianapolis while learning the offense, then appeared to be nearing his debut before a knee injury sidelined him against Pittsburgh last week.
Why Slayton Never Saw the Field
After signing with the Colts on a Tuesday, Slayton had a short week to get up to speed. Ultimately, he couldn’t learn the offense in time, leading to Indianapolis making him a healthy scratch in Week 3. Head coach Shane Steichen pointed to that adjustment period when explaining Slayton's initial absence, saying he needed to continue developing and growing within the offense.
It’s a similar story for the following week against Washington. Slayton wasn’t quite up to speed just yet, so he spent another week as a healthy inactive, though questions began to arise. Slayton was expected to play a valuable role, but hadn’t yet touched the field.
Things were trending in the right direction for Slayton to make his Colts debut in Pittsburgh. But in Indy’s final practice before the game, Slayton picked up a knee injury and was ruled out. He returned to full practice Wednesday, putting him back in contention to play, but the Colts released him just two days later.
What’s Next for the Colts?
Slayton's departure leaves Indianapolis right back where it started four weeks ago, without a field-stretching vertical threat. Strangely, Slayton never made it onto the field despite the team's need, and Indianapolis has opted to move on rather than continue waiting for him to be ready.
One player who could benefit from the decision is rookie Deion Burks. The seventh-round pick has seen limited opportunities through the first five games of his career, but with Slayton no longer in the picture, Burks could have a chance to earn a larger role.
The Colts are also waiting for Alec Pierce to return from injured reserve, which could eventually provide the downfield threat they hoped Slayton would supply. Pierce is eligible to return for Indianapolis' Week 7 matchup against the Minnesota Vikings on Oct. 25, and the release of Slayton indicates Pierce could be progressing rapidly towards an earlier return than expected.
Until Pierce is healthy enough to play, Indianapolis will need its other receivers to find ways to fill the void. The Colts explored a potential trade for Marvin Harrison Jr. before missing out on the former Arizona Cardinals receiver, leaving the team to consider other options as the trade deadline approaches. Several potential trade targets could help address that need, but Slayton's departure leaves Indianapolis still searching for a solution.

title: Colts Must Win These 3 Matchups If They Want to Beat Titans in Week 6
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts are fresh off an all-too-familiar loss to the Steelers in Pittsburgh.
The Colts are 2-3 entering their Week 6 AFC South matchup against the Tennessee Titans, their second divisional game of the young season and first time taking on the Titans.
Tennessee is off a lowly 0-5 start to the 2026 season, and now aims to march into Lucas Oil Stadium on Sunday and get its first win against a divisional rival.
The winless Titans beating the Colts in Week 6 would almost be poetic, given that it would assist the ongoing train wreck that is led by conductor Chris Ballard.
The Colts desperately need to start stacking wins if they want any shot at the division and/or playoffs, and I'm breaking down the three ways they can almost guarantee a much-needed victory against the Titans in Week 6.
Colts' star running back Jonathan Taylor has had a strong start to the season, but he's itching for a breakout game, and what better time than at home against a divisional opponent in the Tennessee Titans?
Taylor is ninth in rushing yards (398) and T-fourth in rushing touchdowns (6), but his career-low 3.9 yards per carry (previous low is 4.4 ypc) screams breakout game.
And the Colts are desperate to lean on Taylor, as their passing offense has become unreliable .
Where the Colts may specifically be able to beat the Titans on the ground is through gap scheme runs, with Taylor's recent success suggesting it's sustainable.
Jonathan Taylor has rushed for a league-high 139 yards on gap scheme runs this season, including five explosive runs (10+ yards), tied for the most among running backs, according to Next Gen Stats. More via NGS:
Taylor has also forced eight missed tackles on gap scheme runs this season, tied for the third-most among backs. Since the start of the 2025 season, Taylor leads the league in gap-scheme rushing yards (726), touchdowns (13), and missed tackles forced (43).
Rushing for 2+ touchdowns in three of his five games is no doubt impressive, but Taylor has yet to rush for 100+ yards, and recent history suggests he'll do so against the Titans.
Taylor's career-high rushing yards against the Titans was just 70 yards throughout his first six matchups, but he's rushed for 100+ in his three games since, not to mention his eight total rushing touchdowns.
It won't be easy, though, given the Titans have a competent rushing defense that is T-12th best in rushing touchdowns allowed (5) and 17th in rushing yards per game allowed.
The Indianapolis Colts have one of the most expensive secondaries in the NFL.
They've rebounded, albeit marginally, since their unacceptable start, but they need to continue their upward trajectory if Indianapolis wants to leave Lucas Oil Stadium with a win.
Titans' quarterback Cam Ward has been one of the worst quarterbacks in the league through five weeks, and Colts' defensive coordinator Lou Anarumo needs to do everything in his power to not allow Ward to have a breakout performance.
Ward ranks in the following categories among qualified quarterbacks leaguewide:
179.2 passing yards per game (2nd-worst among QBs with 5 games played), 3 passing touchdowns (T-25th), 77.2 Passer Rating (28th), 5.8 % Deep Pass Rate (Last)
The Colts' secondary must take advantage of Ward's poor start to the season, especially since the defense has proven to be one of the worst tackling teams in the NFL, its revolving door at linebacker has been a glaring hindrance against the pass and run, and its pass rush cannot be trusted to take matters into its own hands.
Lou Anarumo's defense is 28th in yards allowed after contact (482) and 31st in yards per play allowed (6.8), and even though their tackling woes have been the Colts' biggest concern thus far, their pass rush (or lack thereof) has been doing its best to compete for the title of worst aspect of the defense.
Indianapolis' pass rush has totaled 10 sacks (T-19th), but the Colts' pressure rate is easily the worst (23.7%), as they are the only defense in the league with a sub-30% pressure rate, according to Next Gen Stats.
Furthermore, the Colts haven't been great against the run; in fact, they've been one of the worst, but at least they should be able to take care of the Titans' brutal run game.
Tennessee is averaging just 82.6 rushing yards per game, good for 27th-best in the NFL, and has scored the least number of touchdowns overall (6).
If Lou Anarumo's defense can't handle the Titans, the Colts' season will look even bleaker than previously thought possible.
Trusting Quenton Nelson to handle business is an easy thing to do at this point, but the future Hall of Famer will have his hands full this Sunday when he takes on a familiar foe in defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons.
Simmons is one of the highest-paid tackles in the league, and for good reason. He's become one of the best interior defensive lineman that the sport has to offers, as well as being the Titans' heart and soul of the defense.
Jeffery Simmons has 19 pressures this season, tied for the third-most among defensive tackles, including six quick pressures (under 2.5 seconds), tied for the fifth-most among defensive tackles, according to Next Gen Stats.
Since the start of the 2025 season, Simmons has 29 quick pressures, the most among defensive tackles over that span.
However, the Colts' interior O-line has allowed a 6.3% pressure rate, the 11th-lowest among teams, including just a 0.7% quick-pressure rate, trailing only the Broncos (0.6%).
Nelson and Simmons have faced off twice a season for the past several seasons, and this matchup will begin to determine just how feasible a successful season is for the Indianapolis Colts.
Noah Compton is the Publisher of Indianapolis Colts On SI. Noah is from the Indy area and has been covering the Colts since 2022, including stops at FanSided, The Blue Stable, and SBNation.

title: Colts-Titans Injury Report: Two Colts Starters Make Significant Progress
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts are preparing for a pivotal AFC South matchup against the Tennessee Titans in Week 6.
With Sunday's contest approaching, both teams are working through their final preparations while monitoring several players dealing with injuries. Thursday's practice sessions provided another update on each team's health as the Colts and Titans look to put their best lineups on the field in Nashville.
Let's take a look at the most recent injury developments for both teams.
Indianapolis Colts Injury Report (As of 10/15)
The big news of the day is Matt Goncalves and Jaylhan Tuimoloau being full participants after appearing on the injury report for concussion evaluations on Wednesday . According to James Boyd of The Athletic, neither were practicing in red non-contact jerseys, meaning they are not in concussion protocol. A significant and positive development for Sunday, as both have been evidently cleared and will be good to go this weekend barring a setback.
No practice again for Ashton Dulin. The Colts still consider him week-to-week. Jaylon Carlies missed the game in Pittsburgh and is now in danger of missing his second straight contest after not participating in either practice so far this week.
A number of veterans returned to full participation after getting the day off on Wednesday, including Keenan Allen, Jonathan Taylor and Charvarius Ward. Josh Downs, who was also listed with a hamstring injury on Wednesday, was back in full. Grover Stewart is the only new addition to the report as he gets his usual Thursday rest day.
Will Mallory continues to log full practices, a great sign of his progress working back from a thumb injury. That said, the Colts did sign tight end Pharoah Brown to their active roster from the practice squad earlier this week, bringing the number of tight ends on the roster to four. That’s likely an indication that Mallory is further behind in his rehab than the Colts are letting on.
Thursday's practice report for #TENvsIND pic.twitter.com/cAVnWjK5Lk
Two straight days of full participation for both Daniel Jones and Darius SLayton is a solid indication that both are dealing with minor knocks and are likely on track to play on Sunday. That’s great news for a passing offense that’s dealt with several issues over the first five weeks. If Slayton is healthy for the weekend, he’ll make his long awaited Indianapolis debut unless listed as a healthy scratch on game day.
Limited participation is an improvement for Jalen Travis after missing Wednesday's session. His ankle injury came up during Sunday’s loss to the Steelers, though Travis was able to return to and finish the game. We’ll know more regarding his status tomorrow, but the early indications are at least positive.
Overall, Wednesday’s report brought some worry for the Colts, but Thursday proved to be a significant step in the right direction with several starters either returning to practice or increasing their level of activity. Assuming no new developments arise between now and the final injury report, I’d expect a fairly short list on the Colts’ side of things.
Tennessee Titans Injury Report (As of 10/15)
*-On injured reserve; 21-day practice window currently open
Tennessee’s Thursday report is very similar to the first of the week. All the same names remain, but several players’ participation levels have changed.
Starting with the non-participants, Kevin Winston Jr. is yet to practice this week, indicating he may not be ready for Week 6. Tyjae Spears was limited with a knee injury on Wednesday but was downgraded to no participation on Thursday, making his availability for the weekend unlikely. As a result, the Titans’ run game will lean mostly on Tony Pollard.
Thursday’s Injury Report. pic.twitter.com/aHGH3d327n
Marcus Harris being limited is notable. Tennessee’s starting nickel has been one of the few bright spots for a floundering Titans team, recording an interception and half a sack through five games. David Martin-Robinson is the third of four tight ends listed on the depth chart, ahead of only former Colt Kylen Granson. If Martin-Robinson fails to record a full practice tomorrow, Granson could play a role against his former team.
Nothing much to note with the full participants. Tony Pollard returned from an off-day, as did John Franklin-Myers, and Cor’Dale Flott is on track to play. That said, Amani Hooker didn’t practice after being limited on Wednesday with a concussion. He’ll need to be a full participant in Friday’s practice to have any chance of clearing concussion protocol in time for the game, which seems highly unlikely at this point.
Tennessee’s secondary is the area to monitor as Week 6 approaches. With two starting cornerbacks and both starting safeties dealing with knocks, the Titans could be forced to use some backups.
Considering the wide receiver injuries on the other side for Indianapolis, that could make for a peculiar battle on game day.

title: 3 Burning Questions Facing the Colts Ahead of Week 6
full_text:
There may not be a better get-right opportunity on the Indianapolis Colts' schedule than this one.
Indianapolis is 2-3 and coming off a frustrating loss in Pittsburgh, while the Tennessee Titans enter Lucas Oil Stadium at 0-5 with the NFL's lowest-scoring offense.
This is a game the Colts should win, but it is also a chance to answer a few questions that have followed this team through five weeks.
Moving the football was not the biggest issue against Pittsburgh. Finishing drives was.
Indianapolis scored just one touchdown and settled for five field goals in the 34-22 loss, wasting too many opportunities once the offense reached scoring territory.
The season-long red-zone numbers are actually solid. The Colts have scored touchdowns on 10 of 15 red-zone trips, but Sunday showed how quickly this offense can stall when Jonathan Taylor is not controlling the game.
Taylor was held to 45 yards on 15 carries and did not score against Pittsburgh. Through five games, he has 398 rushing yards and six touchdowns.
Getting him going again, especially near the goal line, has to be priority No. 1.
So far, the answer looks like a resounding yes.
Baltimore, Kansas City and Pittsburgh scored a combined 108 points against Indianapolis. Houston and Washington combined for just 30.
That difference is hard to ignore.
Tennessee now gives this defense another favorable matchup. The Titans are averaging an NFL-worst 11.6 points per game, while Cam Ward has thrown for 896 yards, three touchdowns, and three interceptions.
The biggest key is pressure. Ward has averaged roughly 2.6 yards per attempt when pressured, but Indianapolis has been one of the NFL's worst teams at generating it.
If this pass rush cannot make a struggling rookie quarterback uncomfortable, it's hard to imagine things improving against better competition.
This might be the most interesting question of the week.
Allen played just 11 defensive snaps through the first four games before seeing a career-high 24 against Pittsburgh. For a second-round pick Chris Ballard said would be a green-dot linebacker "from the get-go," his early role has been surprisingly small.
Linebacker has been one of the weakest parts of this defense, and Indianapolis made a clear bet on getting younger at the position this offseason.
Allen does not have to become an every-down star overnight, but Week 5 felt like the first real step toward finding out what the Colts have in him.
Now the question is whether Anarumo keeps the door open.
The Colts have a favorable matchup, a home game and a winless divisional opponent. If they want to get back to .500, these are three areas that need to look different on Sunday.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: Four Bold Predictions for the Colts’ Week 6 Battle with the Titans
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts are heading into Week 6 looking to put last Sunday's loss to Pittsburgh behind them and get back in the win column. A matchup with the Tennessee Titans presents an opportunity to do just that, with Indianapolis entering as the clear favorite against its division rival.
But divisional games rarely follow a predictable script, and the Colts have plenty to prove as they look to build on their iffy start to the season. With another week of football ahead, here are four bold predictions for Sunday's matchup in Nashville.
Red Zone Struggles Will Continue
Through the first five games, the Colts red zone offense has been ultra-reliable. Indianapolis ranks eighth in the NFL in red zone scoring percentage, finding the end zone 66.7% of the time.
But that efficiency took a hit in Pittsburgh.The Colts drove into the red zone on three separate occasions, but only found the end zone once.
I expect those struggles to continue, despite facing a Tennessee defense that’s allowing red zone touchdowns at a 62.5% clip. The Steelers exposed the blueprint the Colts have been using by loading the defensive front with physical run stuffers and keeping gains to a minimum against the run.
With the Colts’ mangled wide receiver core contributing to issues in the passing game, Indianapolis could struggle to find answers when its rushing attack is bottled up. Defenses can afford to crowd the box and force Daniel Jones to beat them through the air, an especially difficult task with limited options on the perimeter.
The Titans have a stud cornerback in Alontae Taylor, who can easily eliminate a pass catcher in the red zone. If the rest of the secondary does its job, and the run defense holds strong in short yardage, then it could be another long day for the Colts offense.
Titans Double Scoring Average, Amplifying Questions About Colts’ Defense
The Titans rank dead last in the NFL in points scored per game (11.6). The Colts defense is towards the bottom of the league in points allowed per game with 27.6, sixth-most in the NFL.
The Colts defensive issues go deep, with allowing so many points being a symptom of the overall problem. Indianapolis ranks near the bottom of the league in pass rush pressure rate and has repeatedly surrendered explosive plays, which have made it difficult for the defense to stay off the field.
Tennessee has struggled to generate offense all season, but the Colts have shown enough vulnerability to give the Titans an opportunity to find success. I expect Tennessee to take advantage of those weaknesses and score at least 23 points, doubling its season average and raising further concerns about Indianapolis' ability to get stops against even the league's least productive offenses.
And as a result, change could be on the horizon.
The Colts' pass rush has been one of the defense's biggest weaknesses through five games. Indianapolis ranks last in the NFL with a 24% pressure rate, struggling to consistently disrupt opposing quarterbacks without relying on coverage or mistakes from the offense.
Tennessee presents an opportunity to change that narrative after allowing four sacks against Houston last week. However, I expect Indianapolis to continue struggling to generate consistent pressure, even against a vulnerable offensive line. Arden Key is on injured reserve for at least three more weeks, and the pass rush is lacking reliable production.
Without consistent pressure, the Colts will have to rely on their secondary to hold up in coverage for extended periods, giving Cam Ward more opportunities to find open receivers. If Indianapolis can't capitalize on Tennessee's protection issues, it will be another frustrating afternoon for a defense searching for answers.
Colts Win, But Unconvincingly
The Colts will have an opportunity to get back on track against a winless Titans team that has struggled to generate offense. However, Indianapolis cannot afford to mistake a favorable matchup for a sign that its problems have been solved. The 34-22 loss to Pittsburgh exposed recurring issues with tackling, explosive plays allowed and red-zone execution that contributed to the team's struggles.
Indianapolis has yet to demonstrate that it can consistently pair its offensive production with dependable defensive play. The Colts can move the ball and put points on the board, but defensive breakdowns have made it difficult to control games when the offense fails to deliver on every possession. Tennessee offers a chance to correct that imbalance, but the Colts will need to show greater discipline and execution on defense to do so.
I expect Indianapolis to come away with a win, but not necessarily the kind of complete performance that quiets concerns about the team's ability to compete with the AFC's better teams. Beating Tennessee is important for the standings. Showing tangible improvement in the areas that cost them against Pittsburgh would be far more meaningful for the Colts' long-term outlook.

title: The Anthony Richardson Conversation Is Heating Up in Indianapolis
full_text:
The Anthony Richardson conversation is resurfacing, and if the Indianapolis Colts keep losing, it is only going to get louder.
Let me make one thing clear: I still believe Daniel Jones is the better quarterback, and I think he can pilot this offense at a very high level once he fully settles back in from Achilles surgery.
But at 2-3, with the offense taking a clear step backward, it is fair to ask the question.
ESPN's Ben Solak recently floated that very idea in his Week 6 observations, writing, "The Colts should play Anthony Richardson Sr."
Solak pointed to Jones' declining arm strength and Richardson's rushing ability as reasons Indianapolis should consider a change. He stopped short of calling for a permanent benching, but the idea is now out there.
Richardson's fall from favor under Shane Steichen did not happen overnight.
After being benched in 2024, including the infamous moment against Houston when he removed himself from the game, Steichen repeatedly emphasized consistency, details, and professional habits.
Richardson eventually got the job back, but it never felt like he fully regained Steichen's trust. That carried into 2025, when Indianapolis signed Jones and opened a legitimate quarterback competition.
Richardson kept things close throughout training camp, but Jones was ultimately the more consistent option and won the job.
He then proved the Colts right almost immediately.
Jones helped Indianapolis start 8-2, completing 68.0% of his passes for 3,101 yards, 19 touchdowns, and eight interceptions before tearing his Achilles in December. That is part of the reason I am nowhere near ready to give up on him.
Still, the 2026 numbers are ugly. Jones is 108-of-176 for 1,021 yards, three touchdowns and four interceptions through five games, with a 73.6 passer rating after posting a 100.2 mark last season.
He is only about 10 months removed from Achilles surgery, and the explosiveness clearly has not completely returned.
That is where Richardson becomes interesting.
His passing numbers are rough: 50.6% completions, 2,400 yards, 11 touchdowns and 13 interceptions. But he is 8-7 as a starter and has added 634 rushing yards and 10 touchdowns.
There is something to be said for what that rushing threat could do next to Jonathan Taylor. Defenses have to account for Richardson as a runner, which can open things up in the read-option game.
The problem is obvious. If defenses do not fear Richardson's arm, Indianapolis becomes much easier to defend.
Jones has real rushing ability of his own, and I still believe that part of his game can return as he gets healthier. So no, I would not advocate for making the switch any time soon.
But if this season starts going off the rails, the Colts may reach a point where they have nothing left to lose. With Steichen and Chris Ballard under enormous pressure, Richardson could become the ultimate desperation swing.
And as crazy as that might have sounded a month ago, it is becoming increasingly difficult to dismiss the possibility.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: Colts Open Week 6 With Several Key Names on Injury Report
full_text:
At this point, Indianapolis Colts fans are probably tired of watching injuries take a toll on this roster.
It feels like the same story we've seen over the last decade-plus, and through five weeks of the 2026 season, injuries are once again making life considerably more difficult for Indianapolis.
Wednesday's injury report featured several notable names, including two players who left practice for concussion evaluations.
And for a team sitting at 2-3, the last thing Indianapolis needs is more injuries to important contributors.
Offensive lineman Matt Goncalves and rookie defensive end Jaylahn Tuimoloau were both limited Wednesday after leaving practice to undergo concussion evaluations.
Whether either player passed those evaluations remains unclear, but both situations deserve attention heading into Sunday.
Goncalves has been a valuable piece of the offensive line, and with Daniel Jones already struggling to find consistency, losing another contributor up front certainly wouldn't help.
Tuimoloau's situation might be even more frustrating considering the current state of Indianapolis' defensive line.
With Arden Key recently landing on injured reserve, Indianapolis needs its younger pass rushers to step up and produce . Potentially losing another body along the defensive front would only make that challenge more difficult.
Linebacker Jaylon Carlies also missed practice with the rib injury that sidelined him against Pittsburgh. Considering how poorly this linebacker room has performed through five weeks, Indianapolis can hardly afford another week without one of its starters.
Jalen Travis was another nonparticipant after suffering an ankle injury against the Steelers.
Perhaps no position group has been more affected by injuries this season than wide receiver .
Alec Pierce hasn't played since Week 2 against Kansas City, and without his ability to stretch the field, this passing attack has looked considerably less dangerous.
Outside of Josh Downs, there just haven't been many sparks from this group. Downs leads the healthy receivers with 20 catches for 249 yards, but he appeared on Wednesday's report as limited with rest/hamstring listed.
Fortunately, Downs participated in individual drills, suggesting the issue may not be particularly serious.
Keenan Allen did not practice due to rest, while Ashton Dulin remained sidelined with a hamstring injury. One encouraging development was Darius Slayton returning as a full participant after a knee injury kept him out against Pittsburgh.
Slayton hasn't made his Colts debut, but Indianapolis desperately needs someone who can threaten defenses vertically while Pierce remains sidelined.
Right now, opposing defenses simply don't have enough to fear from this passing attack .
Daniel Jones was listed with an ankle injury but practiced fully Wednesday, which is certainly a positive development.
Jonathan Taylor was limited strictly for rest, while Charvarius Ward also received a rest day.
Tight end Will Mallory was another full participant as he continues working toward a potential return from injured reserve.
There's still time for several of these situations to improve before Sunday's divisional matchup against the Tennessee Titans. But the bigger concern remains the same.
Indianapolis is already struggling to find consistency on both sides of the ball, and continuing to lose important contributors certainly isn't making things any easier.
At 2-3, this team needs to start stacking wins. Getting healthy would be a pretty good place to start.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: Colts Have Several Trade Targets to Consider After Marvin Harrison Jr. Miss
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts entered the 2026 season with high expectations, but their offense has developed a glaring weakness at wide receiver . Injuries and a lack of consistent downfield production have limited Daniel Jones' options in the passing game, leaving Indianapolis searching for answers.
With the NFL trade deadline approaching, the Colts must determine whether their current group is capable of getting the job done or if outside help is necessary. The team has playoff aspirations, but its recent performances have exposed some limitations that could become increasingly difficult to overcome as the season progresses.
Acquiring another receiver would give Indianapolis an opportunity to address one of its most pressing concerns. However, making a deal is easier said than done, especially for a team that has already made a significant investment in its present roster.
The question is whether the Colts can find a worthwhile addition at the right price, or if they're better off trusting the players they already have.
The Colts have lacked consistent production from their wide receivers through five games. Josh Downs leads the group with 249 receiving yards, while Keenan Allen has 145 and Laquon Treadwell has 157. Tight end Tyler Warren actually leads the team in receptions with 30, highlighting how much Indianapolis has relied on its tight end to keep the pass game afloat.
Injuries have complicated the picture. Alec Pierce, one of Indianapolis' most important downfield threats, appeared in just two of the team's first five games and is out until further notice Darius Slayton, a midseason addition, is yet to play a game as he deals with a knee injury.
Still, the Colts cannot afford to ignore the position as the trade deadline approaches. The team did its research on a possible trade for Marvin Harrison Jr., but he was moved to Houston after Indy determined the asking price was too steep.
ESPN's Jeremy Fowler and Dan Graziano have identified several wide receivers who could be worth monitoring, giving Indianapolis potential alternatives if it decides its current group needs reinforcement.
One wide out that Graziano threw out as a possible trade candidate is Jacksonville’s Brian Thomas Jr. The third-year player enjoyed a breakout rookie season but regressed in year two and has since fallen behind Parker Washington and Jakobi Meyers in the pecking order. While he may be of interest to receiver-needy teams, Jacksonville is reluctant to trade him, especially with their 4-1 start to the season
Another player whose name is generating some buzz is Browns receiver Jerry Jeudy. Cleveland is building around a young core and Jeudy appears to have fallen out of favor with the Browns prioritizing the development of their two rookie receivers, Denzel Boston and KC Concepcion.
Cleveland reportedly set their asking price at a third or fourth-round pick for Jeudy according to Jordan Schultz , but Schultz isn’t convinced they’ll find a partner willing to meet that price. Fowler echoed a similar sentiment, saying “My sense is while they are not actively shopping Jeudy, a strong offer could change that.”
It appears the Browns are simply holding out until they receive a suitable offer.
The third option Graziano and Fowler listed was Chargers’ receiver Quentin Johnston. Johnston has had a rough go of life in the NFL in his first three seasons as drop issues plagued him early on. Now, the Chargers sit winless at 0-5 with a trip to Kansas City on deck before their bye. If Los Angeles is still without a by the time their bye week rolls around, significant change could be on the way.
“Someone the other day mentioned the possibility of a Chargers fire sale,” Graziano said. “Teams will have an eye on potentially helpful players from a Chargers roster that obviously hasn't come together…Johnston is certainly intriguing.”
The price tag for Johnston is unknown, but if the Colts had any interest, a late-round pick could do the trick. Johnston could fit into Shane Steichen’s offense as a possession receiver, but has an $18 million fifth-year option fully guaranteed coming up in 2027.
Working through the rest of the possible trade targets, Rashod Bateman is someone Fowler said he’s keeping tabs on.
“Zay Flowers is the dominant wide receiver in the Ravens' offense, which means Bateman's production comes and goes,” Fowler said. “Bateman's contract is tradable -- he is due $6.5 million this year and $8.25 million in 2027 -- and other teams have had interest in the past. The Ravens are in contention and might not want to move players, but Bateman is at least a name on my list.”
Lastly, Jauan Jennings came up as an option. The former 49ers receiver signed with the Vikings this offseason but has gotten lost in the offense, logging just two catches so far this season. Minnesota is unbeaten and could be hesitant to move anyone. But if the season begins to go the other way for the Vikings, then Jennings could be on the move around the trade deadline.
Jennings’ contract is relatively cheap with a cap hit of $4.3 million, so that’s not an obstacle in the way of a possible move.
Looking at the options listed by Graziano and Fowler, there are definitely some intriguing ones, but there are a number of variables to consider.
Firstly, the Colts don’t have much draft capital to work with in the trade market. No first-round pick in 2027 makes it difficult to justify trading away a second or third-rounder, and with general manager Chris Ballard likely on the way out of his position, the Colts would be wise to hold onto their 2027 picks for Ballard’s successor.
That said, there is a desire to win this season in Indianapolis, so they could choose to throw caution into the wind and see what happens. Considering the options, I don’t think that’s necessary, but there are players available who could be a fit.
We can rule Thomas out right away as the Jaguars would never trade within the division. Jeudy is a realistic candidate to be moved, but I don’t see him being a needle-mover for the Colts.
I personally would steer well clear of Johnston. While a change of scenery could change the entire trajectory of his career, he’s too volatile an option for the Colts to consider when they need proven and consistent production.
Bateman and Jennings are interesting discussions, and the Colts should absolutely do their due diligence on what it would take to make a trade happen. Neither will lead the way as the clear top choice receiver in the Indianapolis offense, but both bring proven experience and solid role-playing production.
Plus, since both contributed to multiple playoff runs with the Ravens and 49ers respectively, Bateman and Jennings both come from a winning culture, which the Colts may be a valuable intangible and something they need to infuse into an otherwise mediocre roster. Still, without a 1,000-yard season between them, the Colts need to try and buy low. With Bateman, I don't think the Ravens would be willing to move him at a low price. With Jennings, it's possible, but he'd most likely be a rental until the end of the season.
All things considered, I wouldn’t rule out any sort of trade on the Colts side of things. The team is in desperate need of pass-catching help. Of the options that are available as of now, none are true building blocks for the long-term, but there are some possible band-aids available to help Indianapolis get through 2026.

title: 3 Jaguars X-Factors vs. the Texans in Week 5: Bhayshul Tuten Can Be the Difference
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- For the Jacksonville Jaguars to continue to stack up the wins during their AFC South race, it will take quite the effort in Week 6.
The Jaguars are set to clash with the Houston Texans in London on Sunday, and it will take high-level efforts from more than a few players to give the Jaguars the edge over their bitter rivals.
So, which Jaguars could prove to be difference-makers once the ball is kicked off in London? We break it down below.
A lot of the talk this week has been around the Jaguars' offensive tackles and their matchups with Texans star pass-rushers Will Anderson and Danielle Hunter, and for obvious reasons. But I think the Jaguars' lineman who could prove to perhaps be even more vital to the Jaguars' ability to pick up the win is right guard Ezra Cleveland, and there are a few different reasons why he could prove to be so vital along with the rest of the Jaguars' interior offensive line.
The Texans have sent four or fewer pass rushers on 78.5% of opponent dropbacks this season, the third-highest rate in the NFL, and have recorded 14 sacks with four or fewer rushers, the most. This means they are set to rely on their front four to get pressure, starting with Anderson and Hunter. But the Jaguars can offer chip help for those two and move the pocket away from them. They can't do the same for the interior, with Cleveland and the rest of the Jaguars' interior linemen set to face Sheldon Rankins (2 sacks, 10.3% pressure rate) and Logan Hall (1 sack, 11.4%). These are two quality rushers, and it will be up to Cleveland to make sure they do not wreck the game.
The Texans are a physical defense that doesn't just play that way in the front-seven. They are going to challenge wide receivers at the line of scrimmage, during the route, and at the catch-point, and it will take a physical brand of football for the Jaguars' pass-catchers to produce. The Texans' secondary has given up a lot of explosive plays, but this doesn't mean they are about to play a soft game that allows the Jaguars to just find space in the backend.
That is why the Jaguars will need Jakobi Meyers in a big way. Derek Stingley Jr. will likely be on Brian Thomas Jr., while the Texans have a terrific plan for stopping tight ends each week. This leaves Parker Washington in the slot and Meyers on the outside. I think the Texans put a good bit of resources into stopping Washington, which leads to the Jaguars placing a clear emphasis on Meyers winning his one-on-ones on the outside. Meyers is as tough and physical of a receiver as they come, and his ability to match the Texans' energy will be key.
We are going with an offensive player for the third time, but for good reason. If the Jaguars are going to beat the Texans, they can not afford to continue to let themselves get into second- and third-and-longs like they have in recent weeks. That is just asking for Anderson and Hunter to wreck the Jaguars' passing game, and the key to slowing them down might come down to Tuten above all else at the end of the day.
"Not a world you want to live in by any means. It puts a lot more pressure on the O-line, puts a lot more pressure on the quarterback, and especially against this defense, we cannot live in that world," Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said Friday about early-down success. "You just look at teams that have had success against Houston, specifically, have been at least on schedule and second-and-seven we can live with. Second-and-10, too often, not a lot of fun.”
The Jaguars have shown an increased confidence in Tuten each week, and now it will be largely up to him and the Jaguars' running game to ensure Trevor Lawrence and the passing attack can be effective. If Tuten can't get going, it might end being a long day.

title: Jaguars-Texans Week 6 National Predictions Roundup: AFC South Hierarchy Officially at Stake
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars know just how much is at stake entering Week 6.
The Jaguars have a long season to go after their first brush with the Houston Texans on Sunday, but that doesn't take away the importance of a rivalry AFC South game that could heavily impact where each team goes from here. As Jaguars head coach Liam Coen noted this week, divisional games offer a chance for a different slate of circumstances compared to typical weeks.
"Know that every time that you line up against this team, it's going to be a fight. It's going to be a brawl. That's what's great about football, that's what's great about rivalries, is that you have a level of respect for each other," Coen said.
"Because you know any given Sunday, anything can happen, especially in rivalry-type games and understanding what you can learn from each of these opportunities that you play against one another in, and how well you start to get to know each other in ways in terms of what they want to do, what we want to do. And that's the cat and mouse game; that's the game within the game that you have to play.”
So with the Jaguars and Texans seemingly so evenly matched entering Week 6, how does the national media see this game playing out? We break it down below.
Albert Breer: Texans Eva Geitheim: Jaguars Mitch Goldich: Jaguars Mike Kadlick: Jaguars Gilbert Manzano: Jaguars Conor Orr: Texans John Pluym: Jaguars Matt Verderame: Jaguars
Pamela Maldonado: Texans Eric Moody: Jaguars Seth Walder: Texans
Jeremy Bergman: Texans Brooke Cersosimo: Jaguars Gennaro Filice: Texans Bobby Kownack: Jaguars Dan Parr: Jaguars
Zach Berman: Texans Jon Greenberg: Texans Larry Holder: Jaguars Chad Graff: Texans Josh Kendall: Jaguars Austin Mock: Jaguars Steven Louis Goldstein: Jaguars
Jaguars get the nod over Houston 14-9, making this their second-tightest voting split this year after their Week 2 game against the Denver Broncos. This is not exactly surprising considering the Jaguars and Texans played each other so tightly two years ago, and considering the fact that so many had picked the Texans to win the AFC South to begin with. Houston just needed one win against the hapless Titans to draw closer to the Jaguars in terms of votes.
I think this will be a close game because, on paper, these two teams are close in nearly every area. The Jaguars have a much better running game than the Texans do, but both teams have talented quarterbacks who are playing well, proven head coaches, explosive pass-catchers, strong defenses, so on and so forth. Even the biggest question for each team is the same (the offensive lines). While the Texans are 1-4, everything indicates this is a closer matchup on paper than one would think just looking at the records.
With that said, I think the fact the Jaguars have been a more complete team this season is no accident and is not owrth simply tossing aside. The Jaguars have been one of the best teams in the NFL this season, and the Jaguars have more things to hang their hat on right now than this Texans squad does. I have the Jaguars 27, Texans 24 in what should be another one-score game that gets decided with a late score or stop.

title: 3 Key Areas Jaguars Have an Advantage Over Texans: Attacking Houston's OL Weakness
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars have perhaps their most important game of the 2026 season thus far right around the corner.
The Jaguars will open their AFC South slate against the Houston Texans in London in Week 6, a game that could go a long way toward determining whether the Jaguars can create a larger gap between them and the Texans in the divisonal race.
So, what areas do the Jaguars have an edge over Houston ahead of Week 6? We break it down ahead of the Jaguars' critical matchup with the Texans.
If there is one area where the Jaguars should be able to clearly overwhelm the Texans , it is in the trenches when the Jaguars are on defense. We saw the Jaguars get after the Philadelphia Eagles' offensive line last week, both with four-man rushes and with blitzes. Whether the Jaguars can do the same against the Texans and CJ Stroud should go a long way toward determining who wins this game.
The Texans, once again, have a patchwork offensive line that has not been able to put it together. The Texans' offensive line simply does not have the talent to match the likes of Josh Hines-Allen, Travon Walker and Arik Armstead in the passing game. Hines-Allen and Walker have had massive performances against the Texans in the past, and everything is set up for them to have the same kind of performance on Sunday.
The Jaguars' running game has been humming in 2026 until running into some hurdles last week, in part due the ascension of Bhayshul Tuten and the contributions the Jaguars' rookies Josh Cameron and Emmanuel Pregnon have made on the rushing attack. The Texans do have a good run defense, but the Jaguars have proven enough with their running game to this point that one could expect them to at least have a neutral set of outcomes against Houston.
As for the other side of the ball, it is hard to imagine the Texans getting anything going on the ground. They once again have one of the worst rushing attacks in the NFL, Woody Marks is set to lead their backfield, and the Jaguars' rush defense is even better this year than it was a year ago.  The Jaguars' defense has allowed an NFL-low 63.8 rushing yards per 
game (9.0 fewer than the next-closest team) and the second
 fewest points per game in the NFL (14.0), and their domination against the run is a big reason why.
The biggest reason the Jaguars are one of the best teams in football right now is Liam Coen. During most weeks in his tenure, the Jaguars have had one of the NFL's most productive and efficient offensive schemes thanks to Coen and his ability as a play-caller. Coen has not been able to put together great offensive games against the Houston Texans in his short tenure as head coach, but he does give the Jaguars a big edge when it comes to play-caller vs. play-caller.
Coen vs. DeMeco Ryans should be a fascinating chessmatch, and it would be surprising if both coaches do not hold their own at different points. With that said, the Texans' offensive coordinator Nick Caley is not quite made of the same stuff. If he has to get into a shootout to both keep pace with Coen and try to get ahead of Anthony Campanile, there is reason to believe the Texans would struggle. The Texans will not want to put this game in Caley's hands.

title: 3 Jaguars Storylines I'm Watching Closely vs. Texans: Liam Coen's Offense Finding Its Way
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- Not much has to be said to drum up interest for this one,
The Jacksonville Jaguars are facing a critical early-season test against the Houston Texans in Week 6, marking their first AFC South battle of the season. So, what Jaguars storylines will we be watching most closely when the Jaguars and Texans kick off in London on Sunday? We break it down below.
The Jaguars' offense put up big points during the first three weeks of the season, scoring an average of 27.33 points and hitting 34+ points twice in wins over the Cleveland Browns and New England Patriots. And while the offense has moved the ball well and has ultimately got the job done over their last two wins v. the Cincinnati Bengals and Piladelphia Eagles, it is also clear the Jaguars are leaving plenty of meat on the bone.
The Jaguars have simply gotten in their own way too often over the last two weeks, from penalties negating touchdowns to woeful red-zone trips that didn't see the Jaguars punch it into the end-zone. The Jaguars have been their biggest enemy on offense over the last two weeks, and they simply can not afford to let this repeat against a talented Texans defense.
"I think anytime you're self-inflicted, it's challenging. Us as coaches, trying to make sure we provide clarity throughout the week on the game plan," Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said Friday. "You don't want to trim too much because we started the season off pretty good, and so it is what it is. We're at a point where we have to get our hands inside more in terms of what we're blocking on the perimeter. If they're going to call that stuff, we have to get our hands inside, and we have to be better about it. But ultimately, you can call a hold on every play.”
It feels like the Jaguars will need someone to make a game-changing play on defense to make sure they force CJ Stroud into the kind of mistakes he has yet to make in 2026. Travis Hunter might be the best candidate to do so considering his ball skills and the fact that he is set to see plenty of both Nico Collins and Marvin Harrison Jr. on Sunday. Or perhaps it will once again be Foyesade Oluokun. Or maybe it will be Josh Hines-Allen or Travon Walker against a weak Texans offensive line.
No matter who it is, the Jaguars will need someone who can make the play that tips the scales on defense. Turnovers can not be expected every single week, but the Jaguars must find a way to make it happen this week to ensure that they get the Texans' offense off track, The Texans are unlikely to run the ball much, of course, which means the Jaguars will likely have to make it happen in the passing game.
It is clear how much pressure is facing the Jaguars' offensive tackles this week. The Texans have one of the best pass-rush duos in the entire NFL, if not the very best, in Will Anderson Jr. and Danielle Hunter; if there was a Defensive Player of the Year Award given out after five weeks, it would likely go to Anderson. Throw in the fact that Jaguars left tackle Anton Harrison won't be playing and the Jaguars' offensive line is facing quite the test, especially offensive tackles Walker Little and Cole Van Lanen.
Little does have a lot of experience and has played his fair share of games against the Texans in the past, giving the Jaguars some confidence in their valuable swing tackle. But the Texans' defense is built around their pass-rush, and they have made other offensive lines pay in a big way in recent weeks, which means Little will need to be at his very best.
“It's really nice having a guy that's played a lot and that I've played a lot with. And I think that position I've seen just over my career, how important that is – if you want to call it swing tackle – that spot is," Jaguars quarterback Trevor Lawrence said this week.
"Unfortunately, Ton's [OL Anton Harrison] going to be out, it happens in this league, and injuries happen. It's an unfortunate part of it. And just seeing how important it is to have a guy that can step up, and Walker's shown that he can do that. I’ve played a lot of football with him. I trust him. He had a great day today, seems ready to go, and he's been locked in the whole season in case his number gets called. So, I don't have any hesitations about him.”

title: Jaguars Get the Eric Murray Update They Desperately Needed Before Texans Battle
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars got some important injury news Friday.
The Jaguars were without starting safety Eric Murray a week ago, but the veteran leader of the safety room is now set to return for an important Week 6 battle vs. the Houston Texans after clearing concussion protocol and returning to full participation practice on Friday.
After missing last week with a concussion, Murray was limited in practice on Wednesday and Thursday before officially clearing the concussion protocol Friday. This means he will return as the starting safety next to Antonio Johnson against the Texans in a pivotal AFC South clash in Week 6, a spot that was occupied by Rayuan Lane last week.
Murray has been one of the Jaguars' top starters at safety since he was signed in free agency last year, and the former Texans safety has made a consideable impact on the defense since joining it. With the injury to Caleb Ransaw in Week 4, Murray's void was certainly felt last week, and would have been felt this week too had he not recovered.
“Eric means a lot to us. Eric is one of the guys you would kind of put him in a classification of he's a coach on the field," Jaguars defensive coordinator Anthony Campanile said last week.
"He's just really good communicator, knows the ins and outs of the defense and can kind of see problems before they start on the field. He's been great that way all the way through, the entire season last season, the beginning of this season. He's been a big part of our success."
With that said, the Jaguars will be missing some bodies in the secondary. Cornerback Montaric Brown has been ruled out for the second time in three weeks with a hamstring injury after he left last week's game against the Eagles after just six snaps on defense. Brown's injury at the cornerback spot across from Trabis Hunter means the Jaguars are down a talented and reliable cornerback, and also means the Jaguars are unlikely to have a cornerback rotation like they did during the first three weeks of the season.
Brown has struggled at times in 2026 due to his injury, but the Jaguars would likely much prefer to have their full depth chart at their disposal considering the success CJ Stroud has found this season. Stroud has yet to throw an interception this season, and the Jaguars will have to be at their best to ensure they can change that.
"I think that C.J.'s done a nice job of taking care of the football and that's just something that you just got to be aware of going into it. It's impacting him pre-snap, post-snap, being able to change the picture; it takes all 11 to be able to do that," Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said on Friday. "We have to be more disciplined with our eyes in general as a defense and as a secondary. So, it's definitely not the week to start being greedy and saying, ‘man, I'm going to be the one to get one,’ because we're trying to be more disciplined with our eyes, especially in some of our man-match coverages.”

title: Jaguars Trade Deadline Big Board: Realistic Targets Ranked by Fit and Cost With Four Weeks Left
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- It is never too early to look ahead.
While the Jacksonville Jaguars sit atop the AFC South thanks to their 4-1 start, that does not mean the Jaguars can't still improve. And the easiest way to do that would be by utilizing next month's trade deadline.
The 2026 trade deadline is still four weeks away, but that doesn't mean we can't take an early peek at which targets make the most sense for the Jaguars, and exactly how much they will cost. We take a look at a few names who make sense below in our Jaguars trade deadline big board, starting with ...
The Fit: I have talked before about why I think Philadelphia Eagles defensive tackle Moro Ojomo is a great fit for the Jaguars. Ojomo is strong against the run, has produced at a high-level as a pass-rusher before, and has the type of explosive skill-set that the Jaguars need to add to their interior defensive line moving forward. Ojomo may be not be a scale-tipper by himself, but he would be a quality add considering his ability to be disruptive and win one-on-ones.
The Cost: This is interesting. If he was under contract for a few more years, it would likely be a Day 2 pick. The fact he is a rental, though, suggests to me he could be had for a Day 3 pick if the Eagles continue to lose games. He would cost virtually nothing in terms of cap space, but if he hits free agency in March he would likely net the Jaguars a comp pick. If the Eagles go into sell mode, I think you could get Ojomo for something perhaps even less than what the Jaguars gave up last year for a then-rental of Jakobi Meyers, who cost a fourth- and a sixth-round pick.
The Fit: I mean, this one is obvious. Travon Walker has had a really good season, but imagine adding Khalil Mack to the mix with him and Josh Hines-Allen and allowing Walker to get more rush snaps inside at defensive tackle. A third-down rush package with Hines-Allen and Mack on the edges and Walker and Arik Armstead inside would be very effective, and Mack would clearly welcom joining a team with deep playoff run aspirations as opposed to whatever is going on in Los Angeles.
The Cost: It has been reported that the Chargers would likely take a fifth-round pick for Mack, which is a deal I think the Jaguars would be comfortable making in a big way. The Jaguars have been very willing to deal Day 3 picks over the last two years because they know they can restock the picks with the compensatory draft pick formula, so this feels like it would be an easy decision for the Jaguars to make. The Chargers just keep losing games, and Mack is one of the players who is the clearest trade candidate.
The Fit: I have mentioned in the past that I am a big fan of Miami Dolphins defensive tackle Zach Sieler, who does have a connection with a few different coaches on the Jaguars' staff. Sieler is not the pass-rusher he used to be, but he does make a ton of plays in the middle of the defensive line, is willing to handle the dirty work, and would fit right in with the brand of defense the Jaguars play. There are better pass-rushers, but he would still give the Jaguars quite the boost when it comes to the trenches in December, January and deep into the playoffs as well.
The Cost: You probably do not feel great if you have to give up more than a fifth for Sieler at this stage of his career, but a fourth and a future pick like they did for Jakobi Meyers would fit into the Jaguars' draft ammo, too. The Dolphins are going to keep losing games, butit does remain to be seen how quickly they will truly give up on this season.
The Fit: The Jaguars have played a bit more man coverage in 2026, especially on the money downs. That is where Brandon Stephens wins, and he would certainly give the Jaguars' depth chart a boost if Montaric Brown continues to deal with the hamstring injury that has limited him in recent weeks. The Jaguars have three good cornerbacks in Travis Hunter, Jarrian Jones, and Jourdan Lewis, but they need one more healthy body.
The Cost: Since the Jets have spent some resources on the cornerback position in recent seasons, it would make sense for them to want to dump Stephens for picks if they keep losing games. Stephens has the kind of talent and a contract that would not hinder a trade, so a fifth would make sense if the Jaguars were desperate, but a sixth-round pick would be the best offer to make for the veteran cornerback.
The Fit: Dylan Cook serves as the Steelers' swing tackle but the young backup does have six games of starting experience. He has been arguably the Steelers' best pass-protector when in the lineup, and he could give the Jaguars a nice insurance option at the left tackle spot if Anton Harrison has to continue to miss time. He might not be seen as a starter in every case, but he would give the Jaguars a better swing tackle option than they currently have with Harrison injured.
The Cost: Normally teams get fleeced when they trade for offensive tackles in season, such as when the Texans traded for Josh Jones in 2023 and when the Jaguars traded Cam Robinson to the Minnesota Vikings in 2024. A sixth, whether now or in a future year, would make sense for Cook, though a seventh would be the most comfortable. The Jaguars could make the trade look a bit like Daniel Faalele's.
