title: Jaguars Mailbag: Anton Harrison, Trade Deadline Takes and the Texans Challenge
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The next month could be very, very interesting for the Jacksonville Jaguars.
Of course, the Jaguars will need to get past the Houston Texans in Week 6 to keep their momentum entering a critical point of the season. In this week's Jaguars mailbag, we take questions on that matchup, where the Jaguars stand entering the early stages of trade deadline talk, and much more.
If Anton is out for the season what moves do you see Jags making before the deadline? Bonus: in your opinion should Travis Hunter be getting BTJ's WR snaps?
A: I think it is certainly fair to wonder what the Anton Harrison injury could mean for the Jaguars' trade deadline plans. The Jaguars do have some depth at the position with Walker Little, and the Jaguars could use he next month to see if Little is truly up to the task of being the starting left tackle moving forward. If for whatever reason the Jaguars think they need to add to the position, I would think they do it. With that said, I am not so sure the Jaguars will be buyers at the deadline because, well, they are playing really good football on both sides. I could see adding defensive line help potentially. Moro Ojomo would make a ton of sense, to me.
And no. Travis Hunter is needed much more at cornerback right now than he is at wide receiver. If any receiver should get more snaps, I think that would be rookie wide receiver Josh Cameron. Until the Jaguars are healthy in the secondary, I do not expect a ton of Hunter on offense.
Liam Coen looked overwhelmed during last Sunday’s game against the Eagles. We saw this in last year’s playoff game. Level of concern, if any?
A: Wach Sean McVay on the sideline in any close game, then feel at ease.
What's the bigger disappointment/worry so far; CVL at RT, Montaric, or Ezra? I feel like all three regressed.
A: Montaric Brown and Cole Van Lanen can be dinged for sure, but both are dealing with injuries. Van Lanen had a serious knee injury in January while Brown has dealt with a hamstring injury for a few weeks. It is unideal since the Jaguars rely on both players in considerable roles. As for Ezra Cleveland, I think he has played OK. He did play better last year, but last year might have been the best year of his entire career.
You think we should run it more or pass it more on offense?
A: The Jaguars are one of the more balanced offenses in the NFL, ranking No. 26 in pass rate and just above the San Francisco 49ers and Buffalo Bills. I think what the Jaguars are doing on offense right now is working, and it would look even better if they didn't get in their own ways with penalties and red-zone mistakes the last two weeks. I think Liam Coen has the right idea for the direction of the Jaguars' offense right now.
How are you feeling about BTJ & his spot on the roster i.e what the team should do? Is it him? Liams system? Every week I flip flop on if we should use him as a valuable trade piece for a pass rusher or is he worth more as a (decoy) deep threat & if another WR went down w/injury?
A: I think if a team offers you a high draft pick, you probably take it. He would be, by far, the best receiver available on the trade market and could reasonably net the Jaguars a top-50 pick. With the way Josh Cameron has played in a limited role, I think you are comfortable making the move if the draft pick is worthwhile. But if a team isn't willing to pony up a significant pick, I do think the Jaguars are better off with him on the roster than off it. He simply draws attention in coverage every single time he is on the field, and the Jaguars can't just toss that aside either. Thomas is a talented player, but his value to the Jaguars really depends on what the rest of the NFL determines his value to be.
Do you think Buster Brown could move to safety effectively? Between injuries there, he excels at zone coverage, our defense has better Man coverage corners in Hunter and Jones (and he's a real liability there) it could be a nice utilization of his skills to get him on the field
A: I think that would be a bit of a stretch. If there is a cornerback on the Jaguars' roster who I think could play safety, it is Jarrian Jones. Montaric Brown is a good player who, for the reasons you noted, could do some good things at safety on paper. But ultimately, Brown is an outside cornerback true and true, and the Jaguars need him to get healthy. Brown has been a good player for an extended period of time now, and it seems clear that he is just banged-up and needs time to get back to being 100%. I would stress patience with Brown right now, while I think the safety room will get healthier here in a bit.
Are you concerned that in the last 2 weeks, the Jags offense has had a chance to end the game with a first down, and has not been able to do so both times?
A: Concerned? No, not really. Each game has its own flow and context. They were half of Parker Washington's foot stepping out of bounds from putting the Bengals down early, for example. I think a bigger "concern" would be that the Jaguars have stalled out too many times before those final drives, thus putting even more pressure on the offense to produce. The Jaguars need their red-zone offense to be better this week by quite a bit, which means relying on Trevor Lawrence's arm.
Now if this is a trend that is still popping up in Week 17 or so, then I think it is time to admit it is an issue. But it is still relatively early in the season, and the Jaguars seem closer to being a good team with their own set of flaws than a team that is scrapping by and just finding ways to win. The Jaguars are in a good spot moving forward.
What’s the deal with kickoff coverage?
A: I think one factor is that the Jaguars simply do not kick touchbacks. The Jaguars have kicked one touchback all season and rank No. 32 in touchback rate at 3.8%. The Jaguars are allowing a lot of return opportunities each week and, thus, are allowing a few big returns in the process. But as a whole, I do not think the numbers suggest the Jaguars are struggling in terms of their kickoff coverage in a big way relative to the rest of the NFL. I think ultimately the special teams unit is a big reason the Jaguars are 4-1.

title: It Is Becoming Clear Which Big-Money Defender the Jaguars Won't Have vs. the Texans
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- It is becoming clear the Jacksonville Jaguars will be without one of their top defenders on Sunday against the Houston Texans, at least based off this week's injury reports.
The Jaguars had two players miss practice for the second day in a row on Thursday with long snapper Ross Matiscik (shoulder) and cornerback Montaric Brown (hamstring). With Brown missing two days in a row, it is becoming clear that the Jaguars will be down one of their top cornerbacks as they face off against the Texans and their passing game.
With the success the Texans have had in the passing game this season, it will be important for the Jaguars' secondary to be at their very best. That looks, as of now, like it will largely be up to Travis Hunter, Jarrian Jones, and Jourdan Lewis to slow down CJ Stroud and Nico Collins . While Brown has struggled at times this season, his last three games have clearly been impacted by his hamstring injury.
Brown missed the Jaguars' Week 4 battle with the Cincinnati Bengals and played just six snaps last week against the Philadelphia Eagles. When healthy, Brown is one of the Jaguars' best defenders thanks to his coverage ability, run defense, and instincts. The Jaguars have a talented secondary that can still make it work and win games without Brown on the field, but they are better when they have their entire unit at 100%.
“Everybody's kind of pulling the rope in the same direction in terms of improvement, and we see that; I've seen that even here in the few days that we've been out here in London. I think the guys are improving, and they're constantly coaching each other on the same stuff, talking about the same stufff," Jaguars defensive coordinator Anthony Campanile said on Thursday.
"And when those things are applied in the practice, it's starting to show up in the game, and their technique has been helping them. They made a bunch of plays the other day. There's plays out there that we certainly want to make but we're making a whole bunch of them, and we're only going to continue to get better. I firmly believe that. And I think it does give us some flexibility, because we got a bunch of guys that have played pretty well for us out there.”
As for those who were limited on Thursday, the Jaguars once again had Tight end Nate Boerkircher (back), right tackle Cole Van Lanen (knee), rookie guard Emmanuel Pregnon (toe), cornerback Jarrian Jones (elbow), cornerback Jourdan Lewis (hamstring), cornerback Jaylon Jones (hamstring) and safety Eric Murray (concussion) listed as limited.
Pregnon is a significant name to watch as we continue through the week. He has started all five games for the Jaguars at left guard and has been a big part of their running game taking a step forward this season. Considering the Jaguars are already missing left tackle Anton Harrison for next month, Pregnon's status entering Sunday against a strong Texans front is critical.

title: 5 Matchups That Will Decide Jaguars vs. Texans: Travis Hunter's Next Challenge
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- For the Jacksonville Jaguars to get past the Houston Texans in Week 6, it will be all about their ability to win matchups.
Matchups are a big reason the Jaguars are 4-1 and leading the AFC South through the first five weeks of the season, and there are several that will decide the result of Sunday's battle with the Texans.
So, which matchups are the most important ahead of the critical AFC South battle with the Texans? We break it down below.
Nico Collins has had some absolutely massive games against the Jaguars in the last few years, and this year it will be up to Travis Hunter and Jarrian Jones to try to slow down the Texans' No. 1 receiver. Each of the Jaguars' cornerbacks has made some big plays over the last few weeks, and they will need to do so again this week against Collins, especially with Montaric Brown injured.
“Nico was at Michigan when I was at Michigan so I kind of know him pretty well. He's a really a big-bodied guy as a receiver, but some of those guys kind of come in the package where they're a possession guy. That's not him," Jaguars defensive coordinator Anthony Campanile said Thursday. "He can run down the field. He can go make plays on nines and eights down the field. He's a guy, they'll hand reverses to him, he's that good with the ball in his hands. And he'll go in there and do the dirty work. He'll block. He’s to me, in every facet, a well-rounded receiver."
Hunter is not bound to travel with Collins, so it will be a team effort to make sure the Jaguars do not see the Texans star make big plays downfield. Collins is going to get his at some point, but the Jaguars' cornerback duo has to provide some resistance.
This one isn't tough to figure out. The Texans are going to rush four and put the onus on the Jaguars to stop Will Anderon, Danielle Hunter and the rest of their pass-rush group. According to NextGenStats, the Texans have sent four or fewer pass rushers on 78.5% of opponent dropbacks this season, the third-highest rate in the NFL, and have recorded 14 sacks with four or fewer rushers, the most. That means pure one-on-ones for the Jaguars' tackles Walker Little and Cole Van Lanen.
“I think how complete their game is as rushers and as run defenders really stands out on tape," Jaguars offensive coordinator Grant Udinski said Thursday. "There are a lot of really good rushers in the league. Now maybe, I don't know if there are as many rushers as good as those two, but there are other good rushers in the league. But it's hard to find two guys who are A, that good at rushing, but B, also that good in the run game, in the screen game. They do all facets of playing defensive end or that position."
The Jaguars' tackles have been up to the Texans' challenge before, but plenty of people probably remember Hunter and Anderson wrecking the Jaguars' offense during the Week 10 loss a year ago. With Anton Harrison out of the lineup, the focus when it comes to stopping the Texans' pass-rush will come down to none other than Little.
If there is a cornerback the Jaguars are going to want to attack this week, I think it is Kamari Lassiter. Parker Washington does a lot of his damage out of the slot, of course, but I think the Jaguars will look to get Washington lined up on the outside against Lassiter when they need to create a shot play downfield. Lassiter has allowed the third-most receiving yards in the NFL this season with 330 yards allowed through five games and s tied for the second-most receptions allowed at 25. Several of these plays have been on explosive downfield passes, and he is the weak link in the Texans' secondary as of right now.
Washington has proven himself as the Jaguars' No. 1 pass-catcher, and he has made big plays against the Texans in past matchups. This is a week for the Jaguars to look to him to make another game-changing play or two, just like he did last week against the Eagles when he scored two touchdowns to lead the way for the win.
Dalton Schultz will not get thrown a million targets like he does in the games Nico Collins misses, but he is still a big piece of the Texans' passing game. I would call him the Texans' No. 2 pass-catcher right now, tying for the team lead in 31 targets while leading the team with 135 routes. The Jaguars will need to make sure they have a good plan for Schultz considering tight ends have had a bit of success against them this year.
Antonio Johnson has been stellar for the Jaguars as a whole this season, but especially in recent weeks. He is the Jaguars' top secondary piece who can effectively stop Schultz from converting first downs and making tough catches for four quarters, and it will be largely up to him and the linebackers to erase Stroud's safety blanket.
“Yeah, we have put a lot on his plate as time has gone by. That started last year, but AJ basically can play a lot of the SAM positions in base. He can do a lot of those things," Campanile said Wednesday. "He does a lot of what the WILL does in base or nickel. He plays the dime position; he plays safety. So, because of that, it kind of lets us do a lot of the same things out of different groupings and hard to tell what position he's actually playing with some of the disguise that those guys have used on the back end.”
The Texans spent a first-round pick on Georgia Tech offensive lineman Keylan Rutledge this April to make him a key piece of their offensive line rebuild. So far, though, Rutledge has had the expected struggles of a rookie offensive lineman. He has allowed the second-most pressures of any Texans' offensive lineman with 14, and this is a matchup that could favor veteran Jaguars defensive tackle Arik Armstead.
Armstead has put together a good stretch of play over the last few weeks, and this game should be one in which he is able to get consistent pressue if the Texans stop attempting to stick to the running game and have to lean on the passing game. Armstead is the key to the Jaguars' interior pass-rush, and they will need him at his best to make Rutledge look like a rookie Sunday.

title: Jaguars Rookie Rankings Entering Week 6: Texans Battle Brings Pressure on 2026 Draft Class
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars' rookie class chipped in to another victory on Sunday against the Philadelphia Eagles, and now it is time to look ahead at how the class is shaping up entering Week 6.
So, what have we seen from the Jaguars' rookies so far after the franchise's 4-1 start? We break it down below in this week's rookie power rankings.
Another week, another healthy scratch for fourth-round rookie Wesley Williams. The Jaguars have had undrafted rookie Bryan Thomas Jr. active over Williams for each of the last four games since BJ Green went down with an injury in Week 1. Williams seems unlikely to play much this season unless the Jaguars run into multiple injuries along the edge.
Sixth-round wide receiver CJ Williams was inactive for the fourth week in a row, trailing only Wesley Williams in healthy scratches amongst the rookie class. The Jaguars have rolled with four full-time receivers in recent weeks, in part because they have had three-to-four tight ends and in part because Travis Hunter is also a receiver option. Williams is unlikely to be active unless there are injuries or some kind of trade in the receiver room.
Albert Regis was a healthy scratch for the Jaguars for the first time in Week 5 against the Eagles, though there is a good chance that was due to the Jaguars having to do some gymnastics for the game day roster in terms of special teams and defensive backs due to injuries. We will see if he is active this week, though it does seem like the Jaguars like what they have gotten from their top-four veteran defensive tackles in front of Regis, too.
While Jalen Huskey was active for the first time this season on Sunday, he did not record a single defensive snap. It remains to be seen if this is going to change or if the Jaguars are going to continue to lean on Rayuan Lane and Kaevon Merriweather as their safety depth, but it certainly seems right now like the latter is more likely. Right now, it seems like a redshirt season for Huskey above all else as a rookie.
Bryan Thomas Jr. was ejected on the first play of the game after a scrap on the kickoff return, but I feel like he would have gotten some run on defense had he played the entire game. Look for him to continue to play a special teams and a backup role moving forward in his rookie season as BJ Green recovers.
Tanner Koziol has not seen a pass get thrown his way, but he has played 16 snaps over the last two weeks after just three snaps in the first three games of the season. That does indicate that his role is increasing a bit considering each of the last two weeks have been close one-score games and not blowouts like when he made his debut in Week 3.
We will have to see if the Jaguars have Nate Boerkircher on the field this weekend against the Texans after he popped up on Wednesday's injury report. He has gotten better and better as a pass-catcher in recent weeks, showing after ability to get tough yards after the catch as well as making a nice catch in traffic in the middle of the field last week. He has been a plus-run blocker, too, though he could always get more consistent there.
Josh Cameron has been one of the most productive rookie receivers in the NFL this season despite not even being close to one of the top rookies in terms of snaps and routes. Cameron has played a limited role in terms of official oppurtunity, but he has also thrived with every single pass that has come his way. Cameron has seen a target on a staggering 30.8% of his routes and he ranks No. 1 on the Jaguars' roster in terms of yards per route on a limited sample size. He is averaging just under eight routes a game, a number that must increase moving forward.
Week 5 was not Emmanuel Pregnon's best game as a Jaguars rookie so far, and I would say that Josh Cameron is inching closer to the No. 1 spot. Pregnon actually held his own more than a few times against the Eagles and was far from the offensive line's biggest issue when it came to missed blocks. The penalties have become a bit of a problem, though, with Pregnon now having five penalties through five games. Only two offensive linemen have more this season. Pregnon is also a bit banged up and was limited during Wednesday's practice. Pregnon has played well by rookie offensive lineman standards if you look at the entire season as a whole, however, and the Jaguars will certainly need him this week against the Texans.

title: Three Matchups the Chiefs Can Exploit Against the Los Angeles Chargers in Week 6
full_text:
The Week 6 matchup between the Kansas City Chiefs and the Los Angeles Chargers looked a lot different on paper back in the summer. The Chargers were fresh off back-to-back playoff appearances and 11-6 seasons under Jim Harbaugh.
Their big offseason splash was bringing in Mike McDaniel as offensive coordinator, a move that seemed like a natural fit with their rushing-attack philosophies. McDaniel built elite offenses out of ones led by Tua Tagovailoa, and now he had Justin Herbert coming off a fourth-place MVP finish at his disposal. They were supposed to be one of Kansas City’s primary obstacles in the AFC West race.
Instead, Los Angeles enters Sunday at 0-5, with an injury report 20 players deep that includes five players already ruled out, one doubtful, and six questionable, on top of eight already on injured reserve. Gone for Sunday are tackles Joe Alt and Rashawn Slater, and safety Derwin James, three of their most important players.
The division race has effectively become a two-team conversation between the Chiefs and the Broncos, with even the Raiders surpassing the Chargers' relevance, and Sunday is Kansas City’s chance to put a firm stamp on that.
Here are the three matchups the Chiefs can exploit most directly.
The sack drought has been well documented . Kansas City has not brought down an opposing quarterback since its four-sack performance against the Broncos in Week 1, and the frustration has been real despite the Chiefs ranking sixth in pressure rate and eighth in quick-pressure rate, according to Sumer Sports .
The pressure is there, but they do need to get home at some point, after ranking dead last in pressure-to-sack rate and total sacks through the first five weeks. There will never be a better opportunity to end that streak than Sunday afternoon.
The Chargers will line up four rookie offensive linemen to protect Herbert, who is a quarterback who tends to hold the ball a little longer than most. In 11 career games against the Chiefs, he has been sacked 30 times with much better offensive lines than this one.
It would be genuinely disappointing if Kansas City does not record multiple sacks on Sunday. Chris Jones, George Karlaftis, R Mason Thomas, and Felix Anudike-Uzomah have been generating pressure all season without payoff, but that should change this weekend.
As fun as it would be to envision breakout performances from Xavier Worthy, Jalen Royals, and Cyrus Allen in the absence of Rashee Rice and Tyquan Thornton , all three are still largely unproven at the professional level. They will see the field, and they could make plays Sunday, but Travis Kelce should remain the most trusted target by a considerable margin.
The 37-year-old has made a career of carving up the Chargers, with 121 catches, 1,474 yards, and nine touchdowns against them. The one safety who has given him legitimate trouble over the years, Derwin James, will not play Sunday due to a hamstring injury.
Without James patrolling the middle of the field, the Chargers have limited answers for what Kelce can do in the intermediate areas. He is on pace for his first 1,000-yard season since 2022, and this matchup should help him stay on pace. Look for Mahomes to target him early and often as he builds trust in his new wide receiver unit .
At this point in the season, any matchup involving Kenneth Walker deserves attention. He led the NFL in rushing with 537 yards through four games, averaging 6.2 yards per carry, while seemingly forcing double-digit missed tackles every week.
Los Angeles is allowing 4.36 yards per carry to opposing rushers this season, ranking 19th in the league. Walker has rushed for over 170 yards in two of his four outings this season, including 177 against the Raiders just two weeks ago, giving the Chiefs a major edge on Sunday.
He took 87 carries through four games, the eighth-most among backs, despite playing one less game than the leaders, but don't expect him to slow down in this matchup. Coming off a bye week with fresh legs, Reid should continue feeding him 20-plus carries.
Emmett Johnson may get more touches as the season progresses, especially now that the bye has passed, but it is hard to take the ball away from the NFL’s current best rusher in this matchup. When you want to win comfortably and keep your offense vanilla against a divisional opponent, you can always hand it to your workhorse.

title: Chiefs Injury Report for Week 6: Rashee Rice, Josh Simmons Game Status Updates
full_text:
In their first week back from the bye, the Kansas City Chiefs are putting the finishing touches on preparations for Sunday's contest against the Los Angeles Chargers. There's also some fresh clarity on whether two of the club's top offensive players will be available in Week 6.
Following Friday's practice to wrap up the week, head coach Andy Reid spoke to the media and revealed that both wide receiver Rashee Rice and left tackle Josh Simmons will miss the weekend.
"As far as the injuries go, Rashee Rice is out for this game," Reid said. "And then Josh Simmons will be out for this game also but has been out and getting better as we go here."
Rice, who left Week 4's win over the Las Vegas Raiders with a hamstring injury , rested during the bye and didn't participate in Kansas City's practices on Wednesday, Thursday or Friday. The team has no plans to place him on injured reserve; Reid believes it'll be a somewhat quick turnaround after the Chargers game.
"Yeah, I mean, you guys saw him out there," Reid said. "He's out there wanting to jump in on everything. He'll be alright. You never know about these. He's a pretty fast healer."
Without Rice and Tyquan Thornton ( ankle ), it'll be players like Xavier Worthy and Jalen Royals looking to contribute out of the receiver room. The recently-acquired Justin Watson and someone like Nikko Remigio or rookie Cyrus Allen could also stumble into some snaps on Sunday.
Quarterback Patrick Mahomes claims to trust whoever his pass catchers are, which Reid echoed on Friday.
"They're excited to get in if they have that chance, and I think they'll do a good job," Reid said. "Pat's got a good relationship with those guys, and that's important. He has some trust there too; that's important."
Simmons, meanwhile, had an extended absence because of a bulging disc in his back . After not practicing since August, the 2025 first-round pick returned this week and was limited each day. Reid said Simmons was "excited to be out there," even without being too involved in terms of workload.
"He got some work in," Reid said. "He didn't work in the team periods. That was the idea, though, that we went out with just so we would get some base and some fundamentals and technique, start getting that."
Elsewhere for the Chiefs, left guard Kingsley Suamataia will get back in the starting lineup on Sunday after riding the pine in Week 4 due to an undisclosed reason.

title: ESPN Matchup Predictor Analyzes Chiefs vs. Chargers Divisional Showdown in Week 6
full_text:
The Kansas City Chiefs should be well-rested coming off their bye , but Andy Reid's squad is getting right back into the action with a divisional matchup against the Los Angeles Chargers. It's a classic example of an unstoppable force versus an immovable object: an unbeaten Chiefs team hosting a winless Los Angeles squad desperate for answers.
KC is among the favorites in the AFC to reach the Super Bowl in early projections. Patrick Mahomes is back to his MVP form after tearing his ACL against this same Chargers team a year ago, and the addition of running back Kenneth Walker has transformed the offense into a juggernaut. Can LA turn its campaign around and pull off an upset in Arrowhead Stadium this weekend? Let's take a look at what ESPN's Matchup Predictor says heading into kickoff.
Justin Herbert and Mahomes have had some great battles over the years, though this matchup comes under unusual circumstances. The Chargers haven't started a season 0-5 since the team was still based in San Diego more than 20 years ago.
ESPN Matchup Predictor Chances at Victory: Chiefs 73.5%, Chargers 26.3%.
Despite their dismal record, the Chargers still have a decent chance of coming out on top Sunday, according to the matchup predictor. For context, before the bye, the computer model only gave the Chiefs a 3.5% greater chance of beating an undefeated Raiders team on the road.
The Chargers are far out of the divisional race and likely out of playoff contention, but Jim Harbaugh's squad isn't as awful as its start suggests. It's hard to imagine a team of this caliber finishing with just four or five wins.
LA suffered inexplicable defeats to the Raiders and Cardinals early in the season. Just when they appeared poised to finally get into the win column last week, the Chargers collapsed in the fourth quarter against fellow AFC West opponent, the Denver Broncos. The matchup predictor gives the Chargers better than a one-in-four chance against KC, suggesting a win may not be too far off the radar for Los Angeles, whether it comes this week or next. The Chargers can't head into November without a single victory... right?
One thing to monitor is the Chiefs' receiving situation, as Tyquan Thornton will be sidelined for an extended period and Rashee Rice is likely to miss the game with a lingering hamstring injury. That means the offense will lean heavily on Walker and Travis Kelce to carry the load.
If the Chargers are going to put up a fight, Herbert has to pick up his play — point-blank, period. It's been a humiliating stretch for someone who is usually considered one of the AFC's best signal-callers, as he's thrown seven interceptions to his five touchdowns in 2026.

title: Chiefs First-Round DT Peter Woods Pops Up on Injury Report Days Before Chargers Game
full_text:
With each passing second, the Kansas City Chiefs are getting closer and closer to their Week 6 showdown at home versus the Los Angeles Chargers. Head coach Andy Reid's crew is hard at work preparing for a bitter division rival to come to down, but the club's injury situation is less than ideal.
Following Thursday's practice, that became even more obvious. In addition to left tackle Josh Simmons and cornerback L'Jarius Sneed being limited and wideout Rashee Rice not participating, another standout player was added to the list.
Per the team on Thursday afternoon, rookie defensive tackle Peter Woods appeared on an updated version of the injury report. The first-round pick is now nursing a neck ailment after not being listed at all on Wednesday when the club had three players (safety Chamarri Conner, fullback Ben VanSumeren and quarterback Patrick Mahomes) deemed full participants.
The silver lining here is there's no reason to worry about Woods just yet. According to Matt Derrick of Chiefs Digest , the neck issue is "not considered a big deal."
Two changes on the Chiefs’ injury report for Thursday: * DT Peter Woods (neck) is added to the report as limited. I’m told it’s not considered a big deal, he should be fine. * FB Ben VanSumeren (thumb) no longer listed. pic.twitter.com/enGJAYpdYt
Woods, the No. 29 overall selection out of Clemson, has played 126 defensive snaps thus far, good for 46% of those available. He hasn't made a sizable impact in the box score, amassing nine tackles and a pass deflection. With that said, the athletic interior lineman is credited with one pressure and three "stops" by Pro Football Focus . Tracking is a bit different on NFL Pro , which gives him seven stops in four games.
Simmons continuing to be a limited participant shouldn't surprise anyone. The 2025 first-rounder is coming off a significant back injury and is clearly being eased back into the fold following over a half-dozen weeks off. Sneed being limited with knee management is a non-story.
Rice, who hurt his hamstring in Week 4's triumph over the Las Vegas Raiders, is a player to keep an eye on. Given that he hasn't gotten any work for consecutive days, it's becoming increasingly difficult to see him being active this weekend against Los Angeles. Reid typically prefers noteworthy participation in the final practice of the week, so there's still some hope, but Rice would have to be brought along quickly.
Once Friday's practice is over with, the overarching takeaway could be whether Woods bounces back and receives a full workload.

title: Three Ways Josh Simmons' Eventual Return Can Help Chiefs Moving Forward
full_text:
Despite being 4-0 after their bye week, the Kansas City Chiefs still have plenty of things they can improve on . As the team heads into the middle portion of its 2026 schedule, help appears to be on the way via the eventual return of standout left tackle Josh Simmons.
The 2025 first-round pick practiced for the first time since August on Wednesday, albeit in limited capacity. It remains to be seen precisely when the former Ohio State star will make his regular-season debut, but it's bound to boost the club in multiple regards once that happens.
Aside from Simmons himself benefitting from being back in the lineup in the foreseeable future, how could it impact Kansas City? Matt Lane and Craig Stout discussed that and more on an October episode of the KC Laboratory podcast on KC Sports Network .
For as promising as Simmons was when playing as a rookie, it's important to remember that the jury is still technically out on him at least a bit. The 32nd overall NFL Draft selection played 94% of available snaps in contests he appeared in, although that overall number saw him active for just eight weeks. He missed time due to a wrist injury and a personal matter, so he isn't exactly the most dependable piece on the roster.
Simmons flashed both good and bad in his debut campaign for the Chiefs. According to Pro Football Focus , his 75.4 pass blocking grade and 18 pressures surrendered on 337 opportunities (5.3%) were sparkling. On the flip side, he struggled with power rushers at times and also earned just a 48.1 run blocking mark from the outlet.
Coming into year No. 2, Simmons outlined his ideal playing weight and goals. It isn't too late for him to still provide hundreds of meaningful reps the rest of the way, but time is certainly ticking for him to prove he's indeed a franchise cornerstone and long-term blind-side protector for quarterback Patrick Mahomes.
Not having the left tackle you planned for can knock any offense off track a bit. The Chiefs have done a fantastic job of navigating life minus Simmons to start the year, but each week shows more and more why he's so important to the sustainability of the attack. In order to string together multiple postseason wins, explosive passes and deeper-developing concepts simply must be staples to make life easier on Mahomes and to threaten defenses.
To this point, per TruMedia , Kansas City has the third-highest share of passes at or behind the line of scrimmage at 32.0%. It's also in the bottom 10 in average yards to the sticks at -1.6, as well as in the top 10 in percentage of throws faster than 2.5 seconds (44.5%). A quick-game passing attack isn't fun for anyone and, more importantly, it leaves infinitely less margin for error. Just ask the 2024 and 2025 Chiefs.
Losing wide receiver Tyquan Thornton to an ankle injury hurts, surely, but the return of Simmons figures to potentially unleash the version of the Kansas City offense that was imagined during training camp.
Just like the reintroduction of any other starting-level player, it pushes everyone else at the position down a rung on the proverbial ladder. For Kansas City, that means undrafted rookie tackle Kahlil Benson either moves to a swing role or overtakes veteran Jaylon Moore for the first-string gig on the right side. The latter is something that many predicted as the offseason program and camp passed — could it become a reality once Simmons is active?
PFF credits Benson with a 44.0 pass blocking grade, a 75.1 run blocking grade and 10 pressures in 143 opportunities (7.0%). Moore's respective grades are 61.1 and 64.1, and his pressure number is eight in 142 chances (5.6%).
During the Week 5 bye, both players were in the top 10 in pressures ceded via FTN 's tracking. Moore's quick pressure rate of 69.2% was downright alarming:
not all pressures are created equal pic.twitter.com/HkagOTdNKc
It isn't like Mahomes is under constant duress; Kansas City's 28.9% pressure rate is the second-lowest in all of football. With that said, the offense is facing the third-lowest share of times blitzed per dropback (24.6%), and it's been discussed how fast the ball is coming out. Simmons and the best right tackle candidate figures to help offset any regression if play calls become more aggressive.

title: Chiefs Preaching 'Trust' Despite Unproven WR Options After Losing Tyquan Thornton
full_text:
With the NFL trade deadline still weeks away but a need at the wide receiver position being present right now, the Kansas City Chiefs find themselves in a strange spot. Coming out of a Week 5 bye, Andy Reid's team hasn't made any major additions to boost the ceiling of the room.
Perhaps the acquisition of Justin Watson can elevate the floor, but there's ample reason to be skeptical of such a prospect. The club whiffed on or simply didn't express enough interest in moving for new Houston Texans pass catcher Marvin Harrison Jr., so the in-house options will be rolled with until the next domino falls.
With no Tyquan Thornton on the field for the foreseeable future, who should Kansas City turn to as a long-term replacement? Is it one player or multiple? Speaking to the media on Wednesday, Reid expressed that he has faith in each person on the depth chart.
"That's the way things worked out for Tyquan," Reid said. "He was having a very good year, and I'm sad to see what happened to him because of that. And he's a great kid on top of all that. But one man's loss is another man's opportunity to jump in and do that. Whoever that might be that's got the call, if they make the play, then that's a positive. But I have trust in all the guys, and Xavier (Worthy) is still in there, too. He's coming off a couple of good catches the last couple of games."
Subtracting Thornton from the equation leaves KC with Worthy, Rashee Rice, first-year man Cyrus Allen, second-year man Jalen Royals, Nikko Remigio and Watson as the main non-tight end targets. Complicating things is that Rice suffered a hamstring injury early in Week 4's win over the Las Vegas Raiders and isn't practicing right after the bye . That leaves his status for Week 6 in question, thus underscoring how dire things could be for the Chiefs.
Can a cast of some shaky vets and the intriguing-but-quiet rookie get the job done versus the Los Angeles Chargers this weekend? Quarterback Patrick Mahomes echoed the same sentiment as Reid, saying his message to the Chiefs' wideouts is nothing but belief.
"It's that they're ready," Mahomes said. "They've put in the work. Obviously, we've had guys in front of them with Tyquan going out there playing great football. They've had to put in the work at practice, and they've been doing that and doing that. Now their number gets called, and they're going to step up to the role and do their job. I'm excited for them. We'll put them in positions to succeed. I have a lot of trust in those guys — a lot of confidence in them — so we'll just continue to push it forward."
Through four games, Worthy is tied for the team lead in targets with 22. He tops the wideout collective with 14 receptions, although both Thornton (219) and Rice (190) who have more yards. Royals' stat line is just three catches for 17 yards; Allen has two targets but no receptions on all of 10 offensive snaps.
If Kansas City has a high-scoring offensive output without Thornton and potentially minus Rice, it'll have to stem from someone like Worthy and perhaps an unsung hero stepping up. With the expectation and standard set at practice, Mahomes thinks the depth is prepared.
"It's going to make it easier for them," Mahomes said. "When you're kind of getting thrown in, you never know which position you're going to be at and what route you're going to be on. It's hard. That's part of playing in the NFL, you don't get those reps that you necessarily would've had in college and high school and stuff like that."

title: Josh Simmons Returns to Practice, Rashee Rice's Status Uncertain for Week 6
full_text:
The Kansas City Chiefs announced a mixed bag of injury news on Wednesday, as two key offensive starters entered Week 6 with injury uncertainty.
Beginning his Wednesday media availability, Chiefs head coach Andy Reid provided an update on wide receiver Rashee Rice (hamstring) and left tackle Josh Simmons (back).
"As far as the injuries go, Rashee will be the only one that doesn't go today," Reid said. "Everybody else is scheduled to do something."
Reid's statement means that Simmons will return to practice in some capacity on Wednesday, marking his first return to the field since mid-August, when he suffered a back injury late in training camp .
On September 30, Reid explained that Simmons has been dealing with a bulging disc in his lower back, which had "kind of hindered the strength of his leg," according to Reid.
On Wednesday, Reid clarified that Simmons still has some hurdles to clear before fully returning.
"We're just gonna ease him back in," Reid said. "Ease him into practice. He's gonna practice, but it'll be on a limited basis."
In Simmons' absence, undrafted rookie Kahlil Benson has played left tackle, while veteran Jaylon Moore has remained on the right side. Reid was asked what the plan would be at right tackle when Simmons returns.
"I haven't even gone there," Reid said. "I'm just glad that [Simmons] is having a chance to come back, for sure. You start dealing with backs, you've got to ease it back in if you can get back in at all, so we'll just see how he does. So I haven't really even gone there. I know [Simmons] has wanted to get back out there, and this is the first step of that."
Rice exited the Chiefs' Week 4 matchup with the Las Vegas Raiders due to a hamstring injury that ultimately sidelined him for the rest of the game.
On Wednesday, Reid was asked if he anticipated Rice returning to practice later this week
"We'll see how it goes," Reid said. "He's actually feeling pretty good as he goes here, so we'll see. Those things, you start dealing with hamstrings, and it could be a week, could be two weeks, you don't know, but I know he's eager to get back in."
The Chiefs are already dealing with one serious injury in the receiver room, as Tyquan Thornton has been placed on injured reserve due to his season-threatening ankle dislocation that he suffered later in the Chiefs' win over the Raiders. As Thornton was placed on IR, the team reunited with veteran receiver Justin Watson , who signed to Kansas City's practice squad.

title: Chiefs On SI Mailbag: Will Cyrus Allen Step Up After Tyquan Thornton's Injury?
full_text:
The Kansas City Chiefs' bye week is over. Now, focus turns to the Los Angeles Chargers. With the Chiefs undefeated and the Chargers still winless, there's a bizarre undertone to this AFC West showdown. Meanwhile, the Chiefs still have uncertainty at left tackle and wide receiver.
Those are the topics we'll begin with on this edition of the Chiefs On SI mailbag .
What happens first? Cyrus Allen reception or Justin Watson reception? -@ReidsNuggies
I'm completely fine with the Chiefs' decision to reunite with Justin Watson on a practice squad basis, but for the season-long health of the receiver room, Cyrus Allen has to start seeing the field more. While Allen has played just 10 offensive snaps, resulting in two targets and zero catches through his first four weeks of NFL action, I do expect him to see an increased workload on Sunday against the Chargers, and I sure hope that includes his first NFL catch.
I could see Watson's role landing in any number of places. It wouldn't surprise me if Watson doesn't see the field for another week or two as he reacclimates to the offense, and it wouldn't surprise me if he took a decent handful of snaps on Sunday as a de facto decoy to keep LA's safeties honest as a theoretical deep threat.
My expectations for Allen's timeline have always been measured—rookie receivers have a learning curve in Andy Reid's offense—but a well-timed bye should help him add a few responsibilities to his plate.
The obvious part about Allen's potential involvement is that the Chiefs simply need one of their receivers to take more reps in Tyquan Thornton's absence. The exciting part is that Allen has the potential to provide much more than a handful of adequate snaps.
Is it Cyrus Allen time in KC? ⏰👀 pic.twitter.com/edTcQOI7Nn
On 3rd and long, what 11 defenders do you want on the field to get the stop? -@youjustreadmym1
This is a great question to cut through some of the challenges of picking favorites (and least-favorites) in a defensive rotation. Some of these picks are easy, some are toss-ups.
George Karlaftis and Chris Jones have to be on the defensive line. I'll leave Jones in the interior, with R Mason Thomas on the other edge. I'm still very bullish on Peter Woods, but right now... Felix Anudike-Uzomah as an interior pass rusher has been one of the more interesting developments of the season! Throw Anudike-Uzomah inside, next to Jones.
I'd be tempted to roll with only one linebacker, but having both Nick Bolton and Drue Tranquill seems almost mandatory, even though Tranquill may be playing better than Bolton so far this year .
That leaves me with five defensive backs: Mansoor Delane, Nohl Williams, Chamarri Conner, Alohi Gilman , and... whoever gives you the best chance in the slot. While L'Jarius Sneed has taken most of those snaps so far this year, I'd be inclined to give Chris Roland-Wallace my final spot against a smaller slot receiver, while Sneed gets the nod in a more physical matchup.
If Josh Simmons doesn’t return anytime soon, what is KC’s plan, and how do they avoid a repeat of the 2024 season? -@jacklerner.bsky.social
I think it's interesting to view the Chiefs' current left tackle situation through the lens of 2024, when the issues on Patrick Mahomes' blindside significantly impacted the offense all the way to the Super Bowl.
In 2026, the Chiefs have really had their share of issues from both tackle positions, but if Josh Simmons does return soon, KC can pick their choice of Kahlil Benson or Jaylon Moore at right tackle while sending the other to the swing tackle role. Without Simmons, of course, that gets murky.
I'm not surprised that we haven't seen him through the first four weeks, but undrafted rookie Diego Pounds, who the Chiefs acquired from the Baltimore Ravens just before roster cuts , had some very intruiging film from Baltimore's preseason. He's been a pure left tackle, so the idea of putting Pounds on the left side and Benson back at his natural right side does excite me... at least until I remember that would require Mahomes to be protected by a duo of undrafted rookies. That's not ideal, but it is an answer.
I can't see the Chiefs making a significant pre-deadline move to acquire a left tackle unless they have lost all confidence in Simmons in 2026 and beyond, and a tackle as good as Simmons almost certainly won't hit the market anyway. The best version of the Chiefs' offense depends on having Simmons back as soon as possible.
Do you think the Chiefs will be judicious with Kenneth Walker going forward? Will they be wary of keeping him fresh for the playoffs? -@toptrevor.bsky.social | Do you think we will mix Emmett Johnson in more post-bye, and should we? -@oscarbobo.bsky.social
Before the Chiefs' game against the Miami Dolphins, I wrote that it could be Emmett Johnson's time to shine . (He went on to have six carries for 17 yards.) Last week, I wrote that Johnson should be a bigger part of the mix after the bye week —this time, for sure! Ultimately, I understand why it's easier said than done.
The Chiefs have a one-man offensive easy button with Kenneth Walker in the backfield; if the passing game stalls this Sunday against the Chargers, my desire to see Walker's workload lessened will be overtaken by my desire for the Chiefs to, you know, win the game.
I stand by the idea that Johnson has proven enough to show that he can be a worthwhile No. 2 back behind Walker, and the team ideally would take a few hits off Walker's shoulders during the middle act of the season, but they'll need to have more offensive confidence in other areas before that can be put into practice.

title: The Jury Is Still Out on Chiefs' Safety Room Following Bye Week
full_text:
Change was the theme of the offseason for the Kansas City Chiefs' defense, especially in the secondary. It wasn't just the cornerback position that underwent a shakeup, either, as safety Bryan Cook departed for the Cincinnati Bengals and was replaced by Alohi Gilman in free agency.
The acquisition of Gilman, paired with Chamarri Conner returning to his more natural spot in Steve Spagnuolo's lineup, seemed to set the tone for a productive and disruptive pairing. For multiple reasons, however, that hasn't been the case through four games.
Lumping in a roller coaster of a campaign for Jaden Hicks and a limited workload for Chris Roland-Wallace does nothing but further complicate things. The bad news is that things must improve coming out of the bye week, although the good news is there's ample reason to believe that'll happen.
Starting with Gilman, the former Los Angeles Chargers and Baltimore Ravens standout isn't exactly lacking statistically compared to his last couple of seasons. Across Pro Football Reference , Pro Football Focus and NFL Pro 's data, his coverage data averages out to 10 targets and six completions, 8.3 yards per target and a 120.6 passer rating.
He's being tried more often down the field (13.9-yard average depth of target) and performing at his recent — albeit underwhelming — standard, but it's the lack of ball production that's really hurting. One of Gilman's main draws is his ability to make splash plays, evidenced by his 28 career pass breakups, six fumble recoveries, five forced fumbles and five interceptions. Four games in, he's been quiet, which is a concern.
Hicks is hands-down the most frustratingly inconsistent player in this group. In some instances, he flies around the field and looks like a heat-seeking missile who's oozing confidence. In others, though, he's lost in the shuffle, slow to react and ends up totally out of place. He leads the safety collective with eight "stops" on the year, yet it's coming with a unit-worst mark in yards per reception.
The low-key player to keep an eye on is Roland-Wallace, who played 190 defensive snaps in 2025, good for 30% of those available in his 11 games played. This year, that number is 55 (20%), and it's hard to see that share going up too much with Conner back. Roland-Wallace has some corner-safety versatility, so perhaps he occupies some slot snaps (he has 12 right now) in due time.
Conner stands out as quite easily the biggest X-factor here. The fourth-year man is in a contract season but started it on the shelf due to a knee injury that lingered for a while. While he was far from perfect in his regular-season debut in Week 4 versus the Las Vegas Raiders, the former fourth-round pick finished with six tackles and made multiple plays that showcased his quick trigger when running downhill.
There wasn't much of a runway for Conner to ramp up, as he played 63 snaps down in Paradise against the Raiders (75%). If he's back to being an unquestioned starter at safety, he'll form a heavy-involvement duo with Gilman and send someone like Hicks down a rung on the ladder. That may assist the latter man in finding the optimal role for his skill set.
Progress isn't linear, which might be the best way to sum up a group that's flashed some good and bad in the first month of the 2026-27 campaign.

title: Here’s Why Chiefs Rookie Cyrus Allen Could Finally Be Featured in Kansas City’s Offense
full_text:
The Kansas City Chiefs' bleak wide receiver circumstances worsened before the bye when Rashee Rice and Tyquan Thornton went down in the same game. While Rice's hamstring issue is minor and shouldn't keep him out long, Thornton will miss most, if not all , of the regular season with a dislocated ankle. Between rumors about a reunion with Tyreek Hill and bringing another proven wideout on board before the trade deadline, KC fans are starved for help in the receiving corps. However, a viable option may be waiting in the wings of the Chiefs' offensive unit.
Remember Cyrus Allen, who quickly transformed into a fan favorite with his strong training camp? There was a time when he looked like he'd be facing an uphill battle for playing time, but a scenario where he assumes a significant role in this offense looks a lot more realistic with the current injury situation.
Allen was selected No. 176 overall in the 2026 NFL Draft and brings plenty of versatility, as he's capable of lining up in the slot or on the outside. He led the Big 12 with 13 touchdowns as a senior, which helped his draft stock skyrocket. A shin bruise during camp slowed Allen's progress and has been cited as a reason why the coaching staff has been hesitant to use him. Before that, though, reporters viewed Allen as perhaps the team's best pass catcher not named Rice or Xavier Worthy.
During the Chiefs' Week 4 win over the Raiders, when the two aforementioned receivers got hurt, Allen only saw the field for five snaps and recorded his first NFL target. That could change now that the coaching staff has a week of preparation to get him more involved.
What Kansas City is truly missing in the receiver room is a playmaker who can make things happen with the ball in his hands. Rice is great in the intermediate game, but he isn't necessarily someone defenses are going to key in on to open things up downfield. And despite Worthy's tremendous straight-line speed, he's been largely ineffective in all areas of the offense in 2026.
Allen generated a lot of buzz in limited preseason action, with the biggest highlight coming on an impressive snag in the exhibition opener. Insiders and other observers have made it clear that he has as much burst and is shiftier than anyone in the short passing game.
When speaking to the media on Monday , head coach Andy Reid mentioned the possibility of Allen seeing increased snaps with Thornton heading to the IR. Those opportunities would only grow if Rice is unable to suit up this week versus the Chargers. "Yeah, I think he would probably work into the mix there a little bit more," Reid said. "He's a good football player, and even though he's young, he's got good ability."
Andy Reid on if rookie WR Cyrus Allen will receive more playing time moving forward: “Yeah, I think he would probably work into the mix there a little bit more. He's a good football player, and even though he's young, he's got good ability.” pic.twitter.com/mMeGf7WVX1
Those words don't necessarily mean Allen is going to see a dozen targets on Sunday, so his biggest supporters should take Reid's comments with a grain of salt. Reid tends to have a level of comfort with the players he trusts to catch passes from Patrick Mahomes, which helps explain why the front office brought two-time Chiefs Super Bowl winner Justin Watson back to the practice squad during the bye.
Depending on Rice's injury status before the upcoming matchup, this could be Allen's biggest chance to earn a consistent role in Eric Bieniemy's offense. If he makes the most of his snaps, even in a limited role, he could earn a bigger place in the game plan moving forward.

title: It's Time for Justin Herbert to Pick a Fight
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers are 0-5 and are heading to Kansas City to take on their division rivals, the Kansas City Chiefs. The Chiefs' home of Arrowhead Stadium is regarded as one of the toughest and loudest places to play in the NFL.
The Chargers are marching into Arrowhead dealing with significant injuries on both sides of the ball. The offense is missing most of their original lineup but are relieved to get some help back in the wide receiver room with Ladd McConkey and Quentin Johnston carrying no injury designation into the matchup. The offensive line looks to be a repeat of week five with the unit being comprised with four rookies, although they played well under the circumstances against the Broncos.
For half of the Chargers starting offense, this will be their first taste of football in Arrowhead. Justin Herbert is now the veteran on the offense, there is not one starter left on the offense that has been in the NFL longer than Justin Herbert and none have played as many games in Arrowhead as he has. It is time for Herbert to set the tone, it's time for him to pick a fight with the Chiefs.
Saying that Justin Herbert needs to pick a fight may seem like a hyperbolic attempt at addressing the struggles that have plagued he and the offense this season. I actually mean Herbert needs to get in someone's face.
The Chargers have always responded to Herbert's emotional moments. The slide to finish off the Chiefs in Brazil or the near brawl when former Chargers first-round pick Jerry Tillery blasted Herbert out of bounds are just a few examples of the emotional response Herbert is capable of sparking.
Style points on the slide. Justin Herbert and the #Chargers are 1-0. pic.twitter.com/tlS89dy1iV
As the veteran and leader of the offense, Herbert can set the tone for his rookie offensive line. The Chiefs are not going to feel sorry for the Chargers as they try to find their footing. Former Chargers linebacker Drue Tranquill, now joined in Kansas City with safety Alohi Gilman, always brings extra heat when playing his former team.
If the Chargers have any hope of taking down the Chiefs for their first win of the season and potentially breathing any life back into the 2026 season, they have to bring the fight to them. There is little question that on the defensive side of the ball, safety Tony Jefferson will bring the hit stick and the Chargers defensive front will fight tooth and nail to stop Chiefs new running back Kenneth Walker.
On the offensive side, all eyes will be on Herbert. If the opportunity presents itself, it would go a long way for the team if he is able to spark an emotional moment in Arrowhead, the offense needs it.
Thomas Martinez has covered the Chargers and the NFL draft since 2022. Born and raised as a Chargers fan, experienced the improbable Super Bowl run in the 94’ season as a child, survived Ryan Leaf, the Marlon McCree fumble and Nate Kaeding in the playoffs. title: Chargers Confidence Meter: LA Faces Another Tough Challenge vs Chiefs
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers have reached a point in the season where every game feels like an uphill battle. Unfortunately, their next opportunity comes against one of the toughest teams in the AFC, as they travel to Kansas City on Sunday to take on Patrick Mahomes and the Chiefs.
The Bolts enter the matchup still searching for their first win of the season after an 0-5 start. To make matters worse, the Chargers are riddled with injuries yet again. Which doesn’t help by any means.
Sunday’s game is another chance for Justin Herbert and the rest of the team to prove they can compete with one of the conference’s best.
Chargers ruled out Joe Alt, Kayode Awosika, Bud Dupree, Tre’ Harris, Donte Jackson and Derwin James for Sunday’s game.
There is no easy way to defend Patrick Mahomes. The quarterback has built his reputation on making plays that most quarterbacks would not even attempt, whether that means extending a play outside the pocket, finding a receiver downfield or turning a broken play into a big gain.
The biggest priority has to be making Mahomes uncomfortable without allowing him to take advantage of defensive mistakes. The Bolts cannot afford to give him extra time to find open receivers. Yet, sending too many defenders after him can create opportunities for them to attack the secondary.
Kenneth Walker III has given the Chiefs another dangerous option, making it harder for opposing defenses to focus entirely on Mahomes. If the Chargers struggle to contain the running game, it could open up even more opportunities. That puts added pressure on the defensive front to win its matchups and on the linebackers and secondary to stay disciplined. The defense has shown it can be competitive, particularly against the pass. However, containing Mahomes for four quarters is a different challenge. The defense needs to create pressure, limit explosive plays and give its offense as many opportunities as possible.
On the other side of the ball, Herbert has to find a way to get the Chargers moving consistently. His arm talent is not the question. The bigger issue is putting together productive drives, protecting the football and avoiding the costly mistakes that have hurt the team early this season. The playmakers on that side of the ball are all banged up, so it will be interesting to see what they can do to accommodate that.
Herbert needs support from his offensive line and running game. Taking what the defense gives him and finding ways to keep drives alive could be more important than trying to force a big play on every possession. The Chargers cannot afford to get into a shootout and expect Herbert to do everything himself.  Getting a win on the road will not be easy, especially against an undefeated team coming off its bye week. However, a divisional win would give them something they desperately need. Momentum and a reason to believe their season can still turn around.
The confidence is low at this point of the season due to the obvious, but the last three games have shown they can battle with the best. For any team playing them, it is definitely a trap game.
With no Derwin James, the Chargers may have a Travis Kelce problem. https://t.co/EIdLbNa4dX
Brennan is sports writer focused on delivering sharp analysis, real-time reactions, and engaging storytelling focused on NFL analysis.  He is passionate about football and breaking down what matters to bring fans closer to the action.  Brennan comes from a family of Chargers fans.

title: Chargers’ Injury Roster Move is Latest Proof of the Mike McDaniel Flop
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers faceplanted beyond all reasonable projections in the wake of the hyped arrival of Mike McDaniel .
Before the public embarrassment , the Chargers gave McDaniel pretty much whatever he wanted in the hopes of pushing the Jim Harbaugh era over the hump and unlocking another gear in the promising career of Justin Herbert.
But it just hasn’t worked, to put it nicely. Herbert looks lost in his own offense and is playing the worst ball of his career and the proof on the field shows that Joe Hortiz and the front office simply aren’t anywhere close to actually building a competitive roster.
The standard, staggeringly bad Chargers injury woes are here too, with the latest roster move just another sign of how poorly things have gone.
One would think fullback injury news wouldn’t be that big of a deal.
Alas, here we are: The Chargers put Alec Ingold on injured reserve , which is expected to put a complete end to his season, both due to the issue and overall performance. The club only has so many IR-return spots they can use, anyway.
Ingold is symbolic of a much bigger problem. A hand-picked McDaniel signing from his Miami days, Ingold was one of those guys expected to make the transition to a new offense smoother, while giving the coach someone with the proper athletic profile to really make an impact in said scheme on the field, too.
Instead, Ingold has been horrendous, hitting on lowlights like this:
Drake Thomas showing the world how you get a starting job as an undersized LB pic.twitter.com/Wmt1kTlAAb
It’s been so bad that Ingold has been replaced by Scott Matlock, a two-way player who has been something of a punchline amongst the Chargers fanbase.
Ingold isn’t the only “McDaniel guy” flopping right now. Guard Cole Strange went unquestioned as the starter after following him over from Miami. He’s been awful, to the tune of ranking 73rd out of 75 graded guards at PFF.
It can keep going. Tight end Charlie Kolar has caught six passes in three appearances and the running game isn’t exactly humming. Keaton Mitchell has carried it 33 times for 135 yards. Rookie draft pick wideout Brenen Thompson has appeared in two games, catching one pass.
Meanwhile, McDaniel has sidelined guys like Omarion Hampton and Oronde Gadsden for these outside arrivals as a bonus bit of insult to injury.
So, fullback injury news isn’t really just fullback injury news in Los Angeles. And when it’s Scott Matlock returning to play the hero, it’s a pretty good sign the Chargers are in deep disarray.

title: The Clock Is Ticking on Mike McDaniel, Sean McVay Holds the Answer for Justin Herbert
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers offense has not been doing well and has not been consistent. The failures on offense are the catalyst to why they are currently 0-5.
Injuries have not helped the situation at all. This week's injury report, combined with the current players on injured reserve ensnares more than half of the original 53-man roster .
The arrival of Mike McDaniel in Los Angeles was met with near-universal praise and excitement. Expectations immediately skyrocketed and the coaching staff did rounds on sports talk shows throughout the offseason hyping up how everything was coming together.
All of the excitement came crashing down in week one when the offense looked lost and had zero timing mastered. The offense has not smoothed out the rough edges and have shown little signs of life. To make matters worse, franchise quarterback Justin Herbert is playing the worst football of his career as are many of the Chargers players.
Where did this all go wrong? Mike McDaniel is a disciple of the Shanahan system that is currently all over the NFL. McDaniel worked alongside 49ers head coach Kyle Shanahan, Packers head coach Matt Lafluer and Rams head coach Sean McVay in Washington under then-head coach Mike Shanahan. McDaniel worked under Kyle Shanahan with the San Francisco 49ers before being hired as the head coach of the Miami Dolphins in 2022.
All of the coaches from that Washington staff have adapted the original Shanahan system in their own unique ways to counter modern NFL defenses. McDaniel was particularly unique because he used a NASCAR version of the offense that utilized elite speed to stretch defenses horizontally and create giant lanes for ball carriers to operate.
McDaniel's offense relied on rhythm, anticipation and timing. He utilized motions and cheat motions in extreme ways to create conflicts for defenders. McDaniel with wide receiver Tyreek Hill and quarterback Tua Tagovailoa took the league by storm.
McDaniel's version of the offense has several pitfalls. The offense is designed to create conflicts for defenders and run and pass plays look structurally similar to use illusion as a weapon, in known passing situations such as playing from behind or in third-and-long situations, the illusion is non-existent.
The hyper focus on speed also limits options for short-yardage packages when all of the linemen are smaller and faster but struggle to generate vertical push. This issue has become abundantly clear for the Chargers in 2026 with how the offensive line is structured.
One of the most glaring issues with the offense in general is when the speed and finesse track stars are not available, the timing of the offense goes completely awry. This may be where McDaniel overestimated the Chargers weapons. LA's weapons are not of the same caliber in terms of speed as McDaniel had on hand in Miami and therefore the defender conflicts, spacing and reads are all not working to same success.
The Chargers are also consistently being hit with negative plays on calls with heavy motion. One of the signature ways that defenses have countered the wide-zone rushing attack associated with Shanahan offenses is by utilizing quick B-gap penetration to throw off the motion man if they can win fast enough but also completely disrupting guards moving horizontally.
The biggest example and wake up call for Shanahan-based offensive coordinators was in Super Bowl LIII when Bill Belichick and the Patriots completely shut down McVay's Rams by completely destroying the middle of the offensive line with five and six man fronts limiting the Rams to only three points.
2026 has not gone well for the Chargers offense and, in particular, quarterback Justin Herbert. The Chargers, with inferior interior offensive linemen, have been susceptible to quick losses both is the run and passing game disrupting much of the timing. The receiving corps is heavily depleted by injuries and has been unable to get open quickly, with the exception of healthy Ladd McConkey.
The NASCAR-style offense has been unable to create conflicts for defenders with deception simply because the defense has been able to see plays coming at them. The play calling has been rather predictable and much of that is tied to Los Angeles' personnel limitations.
The trouble for the Chargers has been rooted in the interior offensive line. There are far too many plays being disrupted in the backfield to find any sort of rhythm.
Sean McVay and the Rams were the first to truly have a unique personnel difference when compared to other Shanahan offenses, a strong-armed quarterback in Matthew Stafford. Stafford was able to access more of the field than a typical rhythm and timing point guard style quarterback. The limitations and the necessity for deception and complexity of the Shanahan system were removed with a quarterback like Stafford.
The Rams shifted to incorporate deeper routes, more downhill run concepts and deeper play action off of a shift to a more downhill running game. Herbert has thrived on traditional play-action passing concepts and many of his career highlights all come off of play action or play-action bootlegs.
Justin Herbert on play action drop backs through 2 weeks... 16/21 (76.2%) Completions 304 Yards 2 TD / 0 INT 149.4 Passer Rating +19.1 EPA 11.8 ADOT Throwing 60 yard handoffs out there, especially in PA. All with the 30th ranked run offense in the NFL. Insane. https://t.co/7imhMkbJKR pic.twitter.com/waRYJl6W5C
Sean McVay adapted and evolved his system and play calling to maximize his quarterback's strengths as opposed to asking him to adjust rigidly to his system. Transitioning from Jared Goff to Stafford showed a rapid incorporation of deep crossing routes in the middle of the field off of play action. This also helped to remove the predictability of the quick passing game.
McVay more recently has also shifted the offense to more heavy personnel usage and the Rams are at the top of the NFL in 13 personnel usage, meaning the offense features one running back and three tight ends. This is also an aid to the downhill rushing attack.
The Chargers do use a similar personnel package fairly often deploying 22 personnel featuring a fullback and two tight ends. The offensive line is banged up and now features multiple rookies, although they performed well against the Broncos, leaning into this concept should be a priority.
The bottom line is, the current offense and design is not working, not consistently at least and Herbert looks uncomfortable. McDaniel has a former colleague from the same offensive tree who adapted the system to a quarterback with a similar skillset to Herbert's. Even Matt LaFleur and the Green Bay Packers have evolved with quarterback Jordan Love to push a more vertical passing game in lieu of the quick game.
Can McDaniel borrow a bit from McVay or even LaFleur and build a different gameplan? Or is it already too late? The offense does not need to be redesigned, but the offensive gameplans could be changed for the offense to look different but can McDaniel find the correct blend? The Chargers hope so.

title: Would the Chargers Benefit from a Chris Godwin Trade?
full_text:
As the trade deadline gets closer, many rumors have been spread around. Some of the rumors have gone around the Los Angeles Chargers , who are staring at a winless record going into Week 6.
The path they are heading in is not ideal to say the least. However they could save the end of the season or stock up for next year. With some veterans succumbing to rumors of being traded, the Bolts could start making some moves.
CBS sports writer Carter Bahns recently noted that the Buccaneers could be sellers, and one of those candidates is Wide receiver Chris Godwin.
There are many factors to consider of course. However if all goes right, this could possibly be a great addition to the Chargers.
The potential fit becomes more interesting when considering how Godwin could work alongside Ladd McConkey.
McConkey offers versatility and the ability to create separation, while Godwin could provide another experienced presence capable of winning in the short and intermediate areas. Having both receivers available would give opposing defensive coordinators another matchup to account for instead of allowing them to focus their attention on one primary target.
Godwin could also help take some of the pressure off the Chargers younger receivers. Tre’ Harris and others would still have opportunities to contribute, but adding a proven veteran could allow their roles to develop more naturally. Another consideration is what Godwin could offer on third downs and in the red zone. Adding a savvy receiver who's practically seen it all is very beneficial.  A receiver who understands how to read coverage, adjust his route and compete for contested catches can be particularly useful when defensive space becomes limited. His experience could give Herbert another target to trust in moments when the offense needs a conversion.
Of course, the Chargers would have to weigh the risks before making a move. Godwin’s injury history is a major factor, and his contract would need to fit the team’s financial plans. Tampa Bay’s asking price would matter just as much. Trading away significant draft capital for a veteran receiver only makes sense if the expected production justifies the investment.
Obviously the decision would need to come down to cost, health and how well he fits the offensive system. A Herbert to Godwin connection would be a sight to see, but it's more importantly because the Bolts need massive amounts of help.

title: Only 1 Rare, Unexpected Justin Herbert Trade Scenario Makes Any Sense
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers won’t trade Justin Herbert. Reportedly, the Chargers themselves have even shot down the Herbert trade buzz behind the scenes when asked.
But this is the NFL. Speculation won’t stop. And superstar trade outliers like Micah Parsons, Myles Garrett, Maxx Crosby, to name a few, are pretty hard to ignore.
Still, those aren’t quarterbacks. Herbert also happens to have a big no-trade clause written into his contract, a deal that also happens to hit the Chargers with wicked amounts of dead money if they do a deal.
But again, quarterback. And that position creates maybe the one scenario where projecting a Justin Herbert trade might make a small bit of sense.
The Chargers aren’t going to give up on Herbert. He’s a top-10 quarterback under the age of 30 when clicking. Unless he explicitly wants out, it’s not going to happen.
Only one scenario is even worth talking about on this front: The Chargers boast a top-five draft pick after this season and can recoup multiple first-round picks in a Herbert trade.
That’s it. If the Chargers want to blow everything up in a full-blown reset and start building around a rookie quarterback contract, then fine. The upcoming quarterback class could be loaded and if they really like one of those prospects, getting potentially multiple first-round picks back in next year’s draft, letting them add two or three first-rounders ASAP, might just move the needle. Ask the Titans how picking early in a "down" quarterback year is going with Cam Ward.
A disclaimer: Trading Herbert is foolish. But a top-five pick, combined with shocking trade offers? That’s at least worth a raise of the eyebrow.
Smartly, the Chargers are far more likely to move on from Mike McDaniel and Jim Harbaugh. Exposing Herbert to yet another coaching change, when that’s been one of the biggest issues of his career to date, comes with its own risk. But it feels unavoidable.
They’re also more likely to move on from general manager Joe Hortiz, because frankly, his record largely stinks.
Better to take more risks with Herbert than roll the dice on quarterback purgatory. The Chargers have been sneakily good at finding great quarterbacks over the years, but that doesn't mean the next one will follow the trend.
Make no mistake, resetting yet again around Herbert is a recipe for disaster. The Chargers organization needs to figure out what went wrong and why, and where Herbert’s head is at as they regroup. But 99 percent of trade scenarios and ideas fall flat, outside of this one unlikely outlier that requires them to keep tanking with the worst of the NFL.

title: Chargers Injury Updates Have Torn 53-Man Roster in Half by Week 6
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers are facing their long time division rivals the Kansas City Chiefs at Arrowhead stadium this week for their final game before their bye week. Los Angeles is trying their best to field a competitive team in Week 6 but the football gods are working overtime to make that a more difficult task.
The Chargers start the week with more than 50 percent of their original 53-man roster either on injured reserve or this week's injury report. LA sent out a mostly rookie offensive line to battle the Denver Broncos in week five due to injuries. The rookies gave a positively surprising performance against Denver. wednesday's injury report for week 6 at KC pic.twitter.com/ItqkPJJEmk
Los Angeles has injuries everywhere, even to rooms and position groups where depth was considered a strength. There are two massive hurdles the Chargers will have to overcome this week if they hope to hand Kansas City their first loss of the season and notch their first win.
The Chargers' receiving room was nearly gone in week five with Ladd McConkey available only in emergencies, Quentin Johnston out, Tre' Harris hurt in the first half, Brenen Thompson out, and Keandre Lambert-Smith was still on injured reserve. The only remaining receivers were Derius Davis, who has been a non-factor in 2026, Marquez Valdez-Scantling and Theo Wease Jr., who was just recently signed to the active roster.

Who will be available and effective in week six is still a mystery. We have have to keep a sharp eye on this week's injury reports.
This is a new development. The Chargers defense has kept the Chargers alive the past three weeks and in large part due to the defensive front putting forth a dominant performance against opposing offenses.
Jamaree Caldwell, Justin Egboigbe and Dalvin Tomlinson all being limited to start the week is a concern. Those three being joined by Bud Dupree, Elijah Molden and Daiyan Henley makes the strength of the team now concerningly thin with Derwin James Jr and Donte Jackson not practicing yet.
The Chargers need rest in the worst way and Patrick Mahomes, Kenneth Walker and the Chiefs are standing in their way before they get to their bye. Will they do so with their first win of the season or staring down 0-6? Managing
